utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court deputy. REGISTRAR: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karavelic. I want to take you back to something you were saying yesterday afternoon just before we finished. You finished your evidence by talking about so-called arbitrary actions by Celo, Ramiz Delalic, and I just want to go to the last part of your answer. You were talking about -- you said that, for example, "if a mission was assigned to him, to stay there for 24 hours around the clock we would not be able to do that. He would have to leave the spot in question to attend to some business of his and he would leave the men alone there and things of that kind." Now, when you said "attend to some business of his," what sort of business were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No particular business, the business that he can do, but I'm not sure what specifically you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that he was away from the soldiers and was going elsewhere attending to other business?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably it was just that or something like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown 65 -- the document under our 65 ter exhibit list number 11? Do you require the ERN?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, the B/C/S is 01850108.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 377.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A document is going to come up on the screen in front of you, Mr. Karavelic. You see the document there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's -- it's an order dated the 11th of March 1993, from Sefer Halilovic to the command of the 1st Corps and the 9th Motorised Brigade and the detachment for special purposes of the Main Staff. The order refers to the transfer of 100 soldiers from the 9th Motorised Brigade to the special purposes detachment under Mr. Zulfikar Alispago. Why -- what was the purpose of that particular order?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to comment on this document. There are several reasons for that. First of all, I was the deputy commander of the 1st Corps at the time. This means that I may not be fully informed about the nature of this document or the true intentions behind this document. As for what the intentions are behind this document, well it was possibly the case that Mr. -- General Halilovic, then Chief of Staff, that he coordinated with the Corps Commander Solakovic to resubordinate this amount of soldiers to Zulfikar Alispago's detachment, which reported directly to the Supreme Command Staff of the BH armed forces, the objective probably being to bring manpower levels up in that unit using the certain amount of soldiers so that this unit could respond adequately to the tasks set it, this unit being a unit that reported directly to the main command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At that stage I think you said yesterday that the 4th Corps -- sorry the 1st Corps had 75.000 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout 1993, it was the biggest corps and the figure you've just given is about right. It was always about 75.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you ever seen an order from the person who was the most senior in the army directed to a specific brigade to transfer a small number of soldiers from that one to another one? Have you ever seen that sort of order before?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such orders. However, if you're talking about what the normal procedure was to resolve problems such as these, and to go about tasks such as this one, then I have to say that normally, there would be an order from the superior command to select a particular number of soldiers to be transferred or resubordinate to another unit. Names would not be specified but the units would be. This was the most practicable thing to do. However, there was always the possibility for a superior officer to resolve the issue in precisely this manner, especially -- he has previously consulted, as is the case here, where there was consultation between the commander of the 1st Corps, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, and General Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason why Sefer Halilovic would have wanted, out of the 75.000 men or soldiers under your -- under the command of the 1st Corps, he would have wanted a group of 100 from the 9th Motorised Brigade to be detached to the special purposes unit?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to comment. I don't have the relevant information. I was at the time the deputy commander of the 1st Corps. I said this would not have been the normal thing to do, but it always remained a possibility. It was not something that could have been ruled out. As for the reasons, the reasons were probably to be found in conversations and contact between General Sefer Halilovic and the commander of the 1st Corps. They must have had their own specific reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard evidence of there being a front line around Sarajevo and there being a series of trenches on the side of the ABiH near the front lines. How were the front -- how were the trenches constructed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours before that I just wonder if that document is going to be tendered or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I move to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's not objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So it's admitted into the evidence and with a number on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P377.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question was, how were the trenches constructed? What was the process?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean generally speaking in reference to the defence lines surrounding the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, the whole city of Sarajevo was surrounded and I'm talking the inner perimeter of our defence. I'm talking about the inner perimeter of the city's defences. So that's where the first line of defence was. It was between 60 and 70 kilometres long. There were connected -- interconnected trenches along this entire line. The depth was an average over 2 metres in order to protect men. This first line of trenches had a great number of exits and entries leading to it, very many underground facilities, storages, both for men and ammunition as well as food. In addition to this first line of trenches, depending on the lie of the land and the general nature of the local terrain, there was also the second line of defence. However, it was not a continuous line. It was not connected throughout all around Sarajevo. I'm talking about the one that was behind the first line. And then there were communication trenches to the first line of defence. There were some very prominent features that were important for the defence of the city, that were important for defending the city from the aggressor's attack. Around these, a third line of defence was constructed. It was not connected throughout, not all around, but it was connected to both the second and the first line by communication trenches. There were a number of underground facilities dug deep, used by reserve units used to store ammunition, reserve ammunition, food for the reserve units and in order to give shelter from enemy shelling. These trenches and these communication trenches were dug along the first line of defence to a large extent, 90 per cent or 100 per cent of the cases, by soldiers. Behind the first line, the so-called work units would often be used to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were work units civilian units?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were work units. Under the law on defence these units could be mobilised in the regular way and used for a certain amount of time for defence purposes and those people were certainly civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the process under the law whereby civilians could be utilised to assist in digging those trenches behind the front lines?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a brief clarification of how this was organised. I'll give you one example. If, for example, a brigade belonging to my corps wished for example to have a 30-strong work unit, in order to do some work for that brigade, this brigade or rather its commander using his own officer in charge of mobilisation had to forward a request to the corps command specifying how many men he required for how long, and what the nature of the work to be carried out was. Once the corps commander received this request, or, rather, its organ for personnel and mobilisation, which was a body within the corps command, they would process this document, and on behalf of the corps commander, this document would then be forwarded to the Secretariat for National Defence. The local office for that specific area, now we are talking about the city of Sarajevo, this was a branch office of the defence ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to put it simply. Once this request was received, and having considered all the specific counts and items of the request, they would then mobilise and prepare this work unit and bring it up to wherever it was required. Whether it was the brigade that had submitted the request in the first place or the corps command itself, depending on what was specified in the document itself. And much in the same manner, the unit would eventually be returned back where it had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How were the civilians in the work unit protected from danger when they were engaged in that work?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was always a certain number of officers around that were in charge of these work units and the work units were in their care, so to speak. And the officer would be seconded from the unit that filed the original request. These had to be responsible officers. At all times, in touch with the unit commander. I mean the commander of the unit that the work unit was performing work for. They needed to know the general situation and how the situation was developing. And that's how the work itself was paced. If there was a worsening of the military situation, more often than not, the tasks being performed by the work unit would immediately cease. This is something that was very much taken into account and kept track of. However, if work was being carried out deep behind the lines, within the area of the brigade's responsibility, well, then they were afforded the same protection as all other civilians residing within the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just described the legal or official manner of engaging civilians into a work unit. What unofficial means were there of taking civilians to dig trenches employed by brigades in the 1st command, sorry the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unofficial means would be anything that is not included by my definition, the one I have just given you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you become aware of the use of unofficial means of taking civilians to dig trenches in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on what exactly you mean when you say "did I become aware." I could answer yes or no, depending. There were very few cases where I was officially informed and presented with an appropriate arguments and proof. This was very difficult to prove. There was information coming in, the security service obtained information on a great many such incidents; if that's what we are talking about, then yes, I did become aware of that being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm talking about, and I want you to concentrate at the moment on Ramiz Delalic's brigade. I'll come to Caco's later.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the deputy commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade, this is something that I must admit to myself, even. I never had occasion to learn, especially in 1992 or even up to the summer of 1993, let alone as late as the Trebevic Operation that he was engaging in anything like that. However, I was given a document today to look at, a document such as I've never seen before, nor was I ever informed about a document like this. One of the assistants for security in one of the battalions of the 9th Motorised Brigade submitted a report to his superior officer about security-related affairs in their brigade, saying that the previous night, about 20 people, and I can't be certain about the figure, had arrived allegedly brought in by Ramiz Delalic to perform work that night, work meaning specifically digging trenches for the purposes of the 9th Motorised Brigades. It was later on that I looked at certain documents and reports by the security service which I had not seen at the time, I must say, that I found a number of sources discussing these very same activities in a similar manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they saying had happened?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the first document that I've just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it said that Ramiz Delalic had brought in about 20 people that night - I'm not sure if they were civilians - brought them in, as I said, to dig trenches. They left the next morning, and so on and so forth. The assistant for security was saying something to the effect that this wasn't right and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P211?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You referred to official and unofficial means of citizens being engaged to dig trenches -- or, sorry, being engaged in work units. Is this document an example of an unofficial or an official means of engaging civilians or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours before the witness answers that question, I've just got another matter to raise. The witness just gave a -- an answer which the interpreter has recorded as saying that he was "given a document today" to look at. It's gone off the screen now. But you can go back up, and I just want to clarify whether that document we are talking about is one of the ones that is on the list. I wonder if the Prosecution could just clarify that for us. It's at line 22, page 8, line 22, that's referred to. It may be it may not mean anything it might I just want if clarify before we move to the documents because it has to be clear which documents the witness is being show shown and which one he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic you referred to seeing a document, the translation said today. Have you received any documents today from anyone?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said these last few days, didn't I? Not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which particular document were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I'm looking at on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, well that answers the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And by the way, this document is not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was admitted on the 4th of March 2005, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just going back to the document, Mr. Karavelic, I think my question was, is that an example of an unofficial or an official means of engaging civilians for a work unit or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours just once again before that's done the witness ought to be given the chance to say whether he -- whether this is one of the documents he saw before. Of course, that might allow a lot of other questions to be asked but when the document is being shown it my submission it should be made clear whether the witness had a chance to see it on a previous occasion or not. So I make that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before, you mean in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Not recently, not before --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Not at The Hague, effectively. Of course, there is nothing wrong with -- with the witness being shown documents if the Prosecutor wants to, and I'm not objecting to that as such. But it just has to be clarified first whether it's a document he looked at then or perhaps in his subsequent researches and, yes, so that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's a reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes but I think he just said it was the document that he first saw here. So I think that one is actually answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So I'll go back to my question. You've told us that you saw this one for the first time here a few days ago. Is it --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, is it as an example of a genre of civilians assisting the military? What sort of document is it? Unofficial, official, something else?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Report by the assistant for security from this battalion, which was sent to the security service in his brigade. So to his superior. It is official. However, it doesn't say anything here. Based on this document, I cannot tell whether this was an illegal way of using the work unit or a legal way of using it. Based on this document, I cannot really say anything specifically for one main reason. It's possible, very easily, that the command of the 9th Brigade had a request which it sent to the corps command and that perhaps this unit was sent to dig trenches based on a request. We have a large number of people here. I said 20. But it states here 40. So it's my mistake. I didn't remember it properly. It's a pretty high number, 40 people is quite a large number. However, this assistant for security in the battalion is at quite a low level. So it's quite possible that he wasn't informed, that he wasn't in on things. So in order to respect the proper procedures, he was sending this report to the security service of the 9th Motorised Brigade Command. However, what you say could also be possible but based on this document, I cannot say whether it was one or the other. I would have to dig deeper in the archives of the federation army and look under these dates and try to find whether there was a request from the 9th Motorised Brigade or from the 1st Corps for this work unit. And one more thing, excuse me. It states here that all these people are registered with the duty officer of the 9th Motorised Brigade, which tells me that this is most probably a legal way of doing it. However, I'm not stating that it's one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about Celo, that is Ramiz Delalic's financial activities when he was the deputy commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, in Sarajevo, particularly in 1993, this was -- well, it's very hard for me to find the proper words in order to clarify this. Simply said, it was confusing. Totally confusing. Not only this aspect but all aspects. There was frequent information coming in different ways, not only about Ramiz Delalic but many other brigade commanders, that they were supplying themselves, trying to get food, ammunition, weapons, and other supplies in various ways. For Ramiz Delalic, perhaps this was a little more characteristic or Caco, I would actually put him first. Compared to others. But many others tried to do these things in a similar way or did them in a similar way. I can give you an example. I think this happened during the spring or summer of 1993. I don't know whether Ramiz Delalic made an agreement with the chief of the municipality of the Centar Municipality or whether this was something that he did on his own or whether the chief of the Centar Municipality, Huso Kamber, did that in relation to him. This is something that only they know. But that was when he gave him 20.000 German marks, simply because Huso Kamber, as the head of the municipality, considered that brigade to be conditionally speaking his brigade, and not a brigade of the 1st Corps and so on and so forth, which would be equal to all the other brigades. When I heard this information over the radio, I came down from the front lines of defence. I went to the chief of the municipality's office. I treated him quite badly. I did myself, personally. So because of this quarrel that we had in his office, this information quite quickly reached Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and a day after that he formed a commission headed by General Stjepan Siber and over the next couple of days, he and his team had to effect a reconciliation between us. I got angry precisely because I was constantly trying to introduce a system, and if the chief of the Centar Municipality wished to give 20.000 German marks to the 9th Motorised Brigade, then he should not have done -- given that money to Ramiz Delalic. He could only give the money to the commander of the brigade, and not to Ramiz Delalic. However, the proper way to do it would be for anybody who wanted to give anything outside of the 1st Corps to people in the 1st Corps, it had to be handed to the logistics sector of the 1st Corps or to the finance sector of the 1st Corps and then the 1st Corps would then distribute these funds according to a system. These funds would be distributed to the subordinate units according to a system.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did Kamber give Celo 20.000 Deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to give you a correct answer. I could speculate or guess, but this would lead to problems of the wrong, irregular or unreasonable conduct of the civilian authorities towards the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Stop, stop?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I want to know is what is your information about why he gave the money. Please don't speculate. I just want to ask you a series of questions so if you please confine your answers to the question.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in 1993, when many were thinking about how to escape from Sarajevo, because the survival of Sarajevo was in question, many wished to have some or one of the brigades linked to them in order to be sure of their own protection, and authority. And this is possibly the reason why Huso Kamber got in touch with Ramiz and he probably, perhaps I mean, I'm assuming, wanted to buy him with those 20.000 German marks, so that he would receive some kind of protection from him or something like that. However, this is not in my opinion the best possible estimate, even if it comes from me. Let it just be one of the assessments, an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Celo keep the money?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The money stayed in the brigade. I know that I requested that this money be recorded in the finance section of the command of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what Celo did with the money?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would need to check the documents, if they acted in accordance with my orders and this was supposed to have happened, then this was money that was used by the command of the brigade. So it's very hard for me to say what the money was used for. But there must be some kind of record in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from taking 20.000 Deutschmarks from the chief of the municipality of Centar, what other means was Celo using to obtain finance for his brigades, sorry, his brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, too, in accordance with certain information, including a call that I had from President Izetbegovic himself, and I don't know exactly which date it was, but I think it was in the spring of 1993, requesting that I, as the corps commander check what was going on, whether Ramiz Delalic and his men, during the night, in certain sections of the town, were forcing people to give a voluntary donation. This way, and this concept of work in Sarajevo, and I believe in other places, is called racketeering. Probably because somebody had this information and managed to complain to the president. Ones I arrived in The Hague here I was able to see some documents from the security service about alleged possible activities of that kind by Ramiz Delalic and a number of his soldiers. However, at the time, no such case could be proved by arguments, nor was it proved at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean by "proved by arguments." You just told us you received a call from President Izetbegovic to speak to you about that very issue. What did the president tell you that Celo was supposed to be doing? Can you go into more details about the racketeering, please?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly what I said before. This is exactly what we discussed. President Izetbegovic was also unable to say anything specific, such and such an address, such and such a number, such and such a person. However, I always asked my own security organs that if they had any facts or any specifics relating to this matter, I told them that they should be prosecuted. No such Prosecutions were initiated. So nothing was brought to trial, and nothing was proved. I know that after the Trebevic operation, after the arrest of Ramiz Delalic, during his trial, after the Trebevic action, I don't know whether there is anything that came to light during the trial or whether anything is mentioned in the judgement by the Sarajevo cantonal Court regarding this racketeering. I did not have the opportunity to follow the trial or read the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify what you did in response to President Izetbegovic's conversation with you. It's a little bit unclear from your last answer. What was your response to President Izetbegovic telling you that one of your subordinate commander was allegedly involved in racketeering?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the deputy commanders. He was not a brigade commander. I answered reasonably, of course, as a subordinate of the Supreme Command. "Mr. President, I will take all steps to shed light on this matter and you will be informed." I tried to shed light on this. The security service made many steps regarding these matters. Most often things would end up with assumptions, without any specific arguments or without any statements by the people in question, because the people in question, although this had happened to them, were not able to provide statements after that, probably because of their own safety. The situation in Sarajevo in 1993 cannot be described. It was confused, difficult, complex, full of uncertainty, and this applied to the whole of Sarajevo, never mind one person, whoever he is, or a group of people, whatever it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To clarify something from your last answer, are you saying that you asked the security service to investigate President Izetbegovic's complaint?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you report back to President Izetbegovic -- sorry, first of all, did the security service report back to you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst other things, you showed me a number of documents from the security service, and you could see what's in those documents from my security chief Sacir Arnautovic. You could see what was in the reports he sent back to his superior command, along his line, to Jusuf Jasarevic, as the number one man of the security service in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I learned for the first time of many facts that are stated there here, when I was reading those documents. Probably there was an occasion when I did inform President Izetbegovic, but I don't remember when, how, because we had such numerous requests of that kind. I had problems to establish the movement of certain mortars around Sarajevo. I could never establish anything for a year. I exhausted my people in order to track these portable mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, we are going to have to speed this up. I'm going to have to ask you to please give very brief answers. My question was did they report back to you? You see what I mean? So could you please assist by giving shorter answers, if possible? You just referred to a document. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P210? There is a document there in front of you now, Mr. Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. It's a document titled "official note," it's dated the 1st of July, 1993. Is this one of the documents you saw for the first time when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is the information in the paragraph that begins on the 29th of June 1993 -- I think that's about the fourth paragraph. Is that consistent with the information that President Izetbegovic gave you about racketeering activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, might I just intervene there? The witness is free to give the answer as he sees fit, but I'm not sure whether he has given any evidence that Izetbegovic provided him, that is Mr. Karavelic, himself, with any information. As I understood it, what Mr. Izetbegovic did was to ask him to make an inquiry. Perhaps there is more to it. I don't know. And the witness can say. But at that stage I'm not sure that Mr. Re's proposition has actually got into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The evidence was, at page 15, President Izetbegovic called him and asked that he check out what was going on, whether Ramiz Delalic and his men during the night in certain sections of the town were forcing people to give a voluntary donation, and this concept of work in Sarajevo, and I believe in other places, is called racketeering, probably because somebody had this information and managed to complain to the president. My question is, is that consistent with what the president told him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The question phrased that way, I don't object to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you understand the question a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I'm not sure. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You told us before that President Izetbegovic had asked you about whether it was true that Ramiz Delalic was -- and his men, during the night, were forcing people to give voluntary donations which was racketeering. Looking at that document, in the paragraph referring to Ramiz Delalic making a sweep around Breza [phoen] at a restaurant, was that consistent with what President Izetbegovic said to you in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document by the security service mentions many facts, and a lot of elements. However, President Izetbegovic spoke generally, and he wasn't specific at any point in time, in terms of mentioning the names of people, the street address and number. But it's possible that the conversation President Izetbegovic had with me correspond to this document. It's possible. I cannot give you the exact date of my conversation with President Izetbegovic. Was it at this point in time, before or after?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just go down the document and it refers to, towards the bottom --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is a document dated the 1st of July, I was still deputy commander of the 1st Corps at that time, which means that when President Izetbegovic called at that time he wouldn't have called me. He would have called the commander of the corps. He would have called me very infrequently, my being deputy commander. So it's possible that this call came after I was appointed commander of the corps, which means that it must have taken place in mid-August or after, mid-August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If he called you in your capacity as commander, as opposed to deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Just go down the document. The sentence that reads, "According to the source, that" quote 'negative' unquote "part of the brigade disrespects the 9th Motorised Brigade Commander Ensurovic because they are in favour of Ramiz, a.k.a. Celo, who his subjects are afraid of." I just want to you comment on that particular piece of information. Is that consistent, inconsistent, or something else, with information you knew at the time about the relationship between Celo and Imsirevic and the men in the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part of the document are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The paragraph that begins, "The source claims that most of the people around Ramiz Delalic are from Sandzak." It's halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The portion I want you to comment on -- just read that paragraph and read the next line, "according to the source, that negative part of the brigade ..." Just read that line. You've got it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My security service is mentioning its source, and this is a confidential source. It is not known what kind of a source it is and what the source is. When they are talking about these elements, --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking you that. What I'm asking you about is the next line, and a part of the brigade disrespecting the commander Imsirevic because they are in favour of Celo. What I'm asking you about is disregard the source, just that piece of information. Now, is that information consistent, or inconsistent with the information you yourself had at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours I object to that question. Your Honours, it's not an academic exercise where the witness should be asked to disregard the source in answer the question that my learned friend's posed, he's asked whether this document is consistent with something he told. He was told. And he's fully entitled, in my submission, to comment upon the source that it comes from because that will be the framework within which he answers the question so if he's got comments to make about the source he should be allowed to make them, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because we heard some descriptions concerning of the date of that document. So there might be some doubts in our mind about the source of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think there is a misunderstanding. The source means the informer, the person who has given the information to security. That's not relevant for the purposes of the question. Mr. Karavelic doesn't know what the source is. It's a security document. I'm asking him to comment upon the information, whether it is accurate, as far as he's concerned. He can't comment on who the source is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, well, let's come to the essential questions that -- just to verify the information of this document, I mean from his own experience, whether he heard or saw something described in this document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The piece of information which I want you to comment upon is that one about part of the -- a negative part of the brigade disrespecting the commander Imsirevic because they are in favour of Ramiz, Celo. What I want you to comment upon is the accuracy of that particular statement, according to your own information at the time.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a simple answer. Based on all the information that I have, and based on my own experience at the time, there is probably some truth to this. How much truth exactly would be very difficult to say. Most people in the brigade, most brigade members, respected and obeyed their brigade commander. That much is certain. Nevertheless, I can't rule out the possibility that to a certain extent some soldiers preferred Ramiz Delalic, who was the deputy brigade commander, over their own brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go down to the next paragraph. In the evening, the people who were led to dig are put into the basement of the day care centre but there are no other types of repression against them and the prisoners eat the same food as the army. People are held at digging far less time than those with Caco. In the last group of quote "men diggers" unquote were a couple of young men had regular military papers, so that their forced digging may in a legal sense be considered as a quote "kidnap" unquote of a soldier. Same question. What can you say, based on your own information, about the accuracy of that particular representation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the document says. Unlike my previous answer to your question, in connection with this, there is absolutely nothing that I can tell you. Unlike the case of the 10th Mountain Brigade and its commander Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about -- this is the spring, summer 1993, about where the 9th Motorised Brigade were obtaining its food and ammunition from?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised Brigade, like all other brigades, got everything that was necessary for the defence of the city of Sarajevo through regular supply routes of the corps. Some of the food that was obtained from other sources was more often than not registered or counted by the corps command. The supplies were modest, and diminutive. So modest, in fact, that it was very difficult to understand why this was so. For example, whenever there was a request by the brigade to supply 10.000 or 15.000 bullets, what would usually arrive was 500 or 1.000 bullets at most. The simple reason being that people had no bullets to send. As for uniforms, there were no uniforms to go around. It was as simple as that. So all over soldiers wore trainers, jeans, that sort of thing. They were all civilians. This may have been the reason that people tried, in a variety of other ways, to get their own supplies. If they did this in order to obtain food, ammunition and clothes, this would have been justified. If they were doing this for their own personal gain, it would by no means have been justified. Whatever was done outside the system was usually not recorded or reported, which would seem to make it illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Ramiz Delalic obtaining weaponry and ammunition outside of the regular supply chain?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer that. I don't have a single shred of evidence. If I had, I would certainly make sure he's prosecuted for it. For example, back then, I had two officers, one of them was alleged to have been involved in arms smuggling. This was the assistant for logistics, Eso Radeljas, and the other was Enes Crna, who was reselling certain amounts of coffee. Late in 1993 I had both these officers imprisoned for a period of seven days I had proceedings instituted against them. But I had proof, I had facts that I could pursue, despite which, they were eventually acquitted. Seven days later, they were released from prison and several months later, one of them was acquitted and the other, I think, was imposed a sentence on probation. But this is just one example that I'm giving you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You just said that you didn't have a "single shred of evidence" in relation to Celo but you had facts in relation to the other two men. Did you -- were allegations plead to you about Celo as opposed to you being provided with hard evidence?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More often than not, it was my assistant for security that reported to me about these matters. He would inform me about whatever he believed was relevant in relation to Celo as well as in relation to these other two officers and the entire corps. I've been telling you about how many times I talked to my assistant for security Sacir Arnautovic. If we go back to these two officers that I've mentioned, the two Majors, I said, "Are you sure about the facts? Are you sure about the evidence? Are you sure these people are guilty?" And he invariably said "Yes." But it proved to be very flimsy once the proceedings were under way, in terms of proof, and producing actual evidence. What I'm trying to say is that throughout the war in Sarajevo and in 1993 particularly, there were so many stories going around, so many unfounded stories going around, but I can't say that there weren't stories at one point in time that had something more to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just intervene for one moment here, this is not an objection it's a possible interpretation issue, two of them of the. Firstly at page 25, line 20, the witness mentioned the name of Sacir Arnautovic, the transcript doesn't seem to have quite caught it and I think it's -- perhaps that could be clarified. It is at line 20. So it's spelt the same way as the other witness who came here, but he's not the same one. But anyway, that could be clarified perhaps. The other one was that the Bosnian speakers at -- at -- at our table thought that the interpreters might have missed something that the -- that the witness said. He mentioned two people -- the witness mentioned two people that he had -- that he had initiated proceedings against, with respect to coffee, and with respect to coffee at least, and I'm instructed that the witness may have mentioned the units that they came from, and that doesn't appear on the transcript. Now, that's -- obviously this is on the run but we have to point it out now, otherwise it will just vanish, so I'm sorry to jump into Mr. Re's cross -- sorry, evidence-in-chief there but those things have been pointed out to me so I thought I just better raise them now to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Re, could you have those two points clarified?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first one, Sacir Arnautovic, that will of course be picked up as the transcript is revised because the stenographer has a list of names. The second one, the two -- did you mention the names of the two units from those -- in relation to the coffee smuggler and the weapons smuggler, or the alleged smugglers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eso Radeljas was a major. He was an assistant for logistics alleged to have involved in arms smuggling. This was in the 2nd Vitez Motorised Brigade. I think I said that. And the other man was Major Enes Crna, a commander of a battalion in the 102nd Motorised Brigade at Stup. My security service started proceedings against him for the alleged crime of coffee smuggling. I approved these proceedings. At the time, one kilo of coffee in Sarajevo used to -- the going rate was about 50 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any information linking Ramiz Delalic with criminal activities, such as smuggling?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I answered that already. From time to time I would receive such information. I was in possession of such information to a greater or lesser extent, not only in relation to Ramiz Delalic but to other people too. Sometimes more about Ramiz Delalic than about other people. But Caco was the most prominent. I think he was the number one. However, I did not start any proceedings against Ramiz Delalic. I didn't and my security service didn't, regardless of me, and this speaks for itself. All I'm trying to say is that for different reasons this was not possible. There was a war on or perhaps on account of some other circumstances that I wasn't aware of. The result was it was simply impossible to institute proceedings against him, to prosecute him, or at least it was impossible before the Trebevic operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why was it impossible before the Trebevic operation to take -- to institute proceedings against Ramiz Delalic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to provide a specific answer. Probably because it was impossible to prove the allegations. If you take that into account, it may lead you to other conclusions and other speculations, but this is not something that I wish to venture upon right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just going back to the information about smuggling, you said "from time to time I would receive such information," and said "Caco was number one." Where would you rank Celo on the list of alleged smugglers, two, three, four, five, somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caco was certainly number one. I don't think I would allow myself to put together a ranking now but it wasn't only Ramiz Delalic. There were complaints about other people too. Those two officers that I mentioned. There were complaints coming in about the 4th Motorised Brigade, about Fikret Prevljak. There were complaints about -- well, depending on the case in hand, but there were complaints about a great deal of other commanders. The war went on for four years, as you know, all sorts of things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the complaints about Celo's smuggling? What was he supposed to have been smuggling?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything boils down to arms smuggling and ammunition. Food and equipment for the army, and money. Everything revolves around these things, and I mean everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How was he supposed to -- or how was he alleged to have been smuggling these things?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it's very difficult for me to speak about these things before a court. I may end up saying something that is unfounded. If we are talking about a general feature of the BH army as a whole, equipment, food, ammunition, and weapons were being obtained for the purposes of the armed forces. By what means? By any means available. We bought -- we seized and requisitioned these things from the enemy. There were donations from outside the country that reached us through individuals or bodies inside the country and so on and so forth. Now, in all of this, I'm talking specifically about Ramiz Delalic, whether some people jumped on the band wagon and in what way exactly? Did they derive personal profit? I never managed to prove this and I don't think it's likely ever to be proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to go back to Celo about -- you said you had information or were told that Celo was alleged to have been smuggling. What were you told that he was doing and how he was doing it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, there is one thing that I read in a document these days. Was it just Caco or also Celo? But it was just on the eve of the Trebevic operation in August or September 1993. They managed to obtain a huge amount of anti-tank missiles and the type was Red Arrow TF 8. Is this allegation true? Did they actually manage to obtain this or not? I don't know. I didn't know about it at the time. It was only several days ago that I read about this. But this was never proved because had they been in possession of a considerable amount of these Red Arrow missiles they would have had to surface somewhere once the Trebevic operation was over and done with. But the same sort of stories were going around about all other kinds of equipment, ammunition, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the tunnel under Sarajevo airport being used for?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Including? And meaning?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have just been talking about smuggling. Is smuggling included in everything?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there was smuggling, then I would definitely include it in everything. The DB tunnel, the Dobrinja Butmir tunnel, was the one that caused me the greatest amount of problems in 1993 and 1994. There were so many problems, in fact, that in mid-1994 I got together with President Izetbegovic and he ordered me to hand the tunnel over to be under his control, that is under the control of the executive board of Sarajevo city. I complied.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just go back to spring, summer, 1993. Did you have any information that soldiers within the 1st Corps were using the tunnel for smuggling purposes?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tunnel was not being used at this time. It was only being used from the 1st of August 1993, because that's when it was dug.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant from summer, the 1st of August. Disregard spring.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to state something like that categorically, especially as regards the early days. When the tunnel was first dug, right off we imposed severe restrictions on its use, and on security. That's one thing. On the other hand, I set up a battalion as a security unit for the tunnel and they were supposed to see to it that the tunnel was being used in the proper way. There was so much work involved in this that the first commander, and if I'm not mistaken his name Almir Sutrovic, I'm not sure about his first name, though, so he was the tunnel commander. And after a very short time, he simply ran away. He upped sticks and left. He disappeared. But my sources say he lives in Israel now. Now, I'm just asking the question: Why did he leave? Why did he run away? If this commander ran away, then anything would have been possible, literally anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Historically that's interesting but what I'm trying to get to is did you have any information that soldiers in your corps were involved in smuggling there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing to confirm the stories but there were stories going around, yes. No hard evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they -- what were you told the soldiers were doing in that tunnel and who were they?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is an example for you. I can talk about this until the cows come home because the examples are countless. One morning I was called again by President Izetbegovic. He criticised me severely. He lashed out at me. He had been told that during the night, several hundreds of litres of alcohol had been smuggled out through the tunnel or rather smuggled into the city of Sarajevo. He said, well, Karavelic, shall we now have alcohol passing through this tunnel instead of food, weapons, ammunition and all the things that we really need? My answer was -- but I'm telling it to you like it was. I don't want you to get the wrong idea. I was a very responsible corps commander. I'll take all the measures I can. I got the civilian police forces involved to work along side my own security people. A month later roughly speaking I received word, something to the effect that the civilian police had taken over. There was something to do with this. Alija Izetbegovic knows about this. There is no need to press this any further. What am I -- just one example. There you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. But specifically, were you ever given any information that Celo or Caco were involved in smuggling things through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing major they could have done in a legal sense while using the tunnel. Even if they had done something like that, it could only have been something minor. There was no way to do anything major using that tunnel without this being observed. If we are talking about something that a man could carry on his back or perhaps two or three individuals as a group, it would have been very difficult to control and monitor at the time if not actually impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that a suitable time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will make a break and resume at 11:00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Karavelic. We are going to try and speed this up a little bit if we can to try to get you back to Sarajevo as quickly as possible. All right. So I'll try and ask you very short questions and if you could please help, we might be able to get you home a little bit earlier. I want to get you back to the question I was asking you before the break which was about information about Caco, Celo and that tunnel. I just want to know if you had any information about them using the tunnel, either of them, for smuggling, and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was such information, but I cannot really state any specific one here because I don't have access to them. They are not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is your memory of the information you were given at the time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, Caco passed through the tunnel last night, he created some minor problems, would not submit to control at the entrance to the tunnel, he passed with his five soldiers through the tunnel and then there would be an assessment, it is believed that he brought in this and he brought in that and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what about Celo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less the same, but to a lesser degree, and less frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Celo or Caco have any legitimate reason to be using that tunnel to enter or leave Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, it would be going in or out for some other justified reasons but there were also entries and exits without my knowledge, and even without my approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they require your approval to leave Sarajevo or the approval of someone in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commanders had to have my permission. However, Caco did not adhere to this quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your response to being told that Celo or Caco had been using the tunnel at night? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would order the security service to check whether there were any illegal activities involved and I would simply go on. My objective was the combat, the defence of Sarajevo, and not so much to deal with individuals, no matter who these individuals might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Celo and the commanders of the other units in the 1st Corps? What I mean is, what was the quality of their relationship?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1992 and 1993, and now I'm speaking about the 1st Corps even though I wasn't the commander then, we had some kind of animosity between the brigades in the centre of the Novi Grad and Novo Sarajevo or Ilidza municipalities, in relation to brigades that were located in the municipalities of Centar and Stari Grad. We undertook various activities like socialising and commanders visiting each other so that they would get to know each other better, and create a more harmonious and better internal system of defence as a whole in the 1st Corps. This functioned up until -- well, it's hard for me to give the exact date, but let's say up until the spring of 1993. After that, there was some -- there was even greater animosity that started to appear. For example, I had considerable problems when we are speaking about Ramiz Delalic and his relations with the sabotage, reconnaissance unit. This was a brigade which was also linked to the 1st Corps command headed by Boris Krstanovic, Cile. So there were several occasions when I personally had to deal with resolving their personal conflicts which then grew into conflicts between a large number of soldiers on each side, and even a conflict between the brigades themselves, and there was a conflict like that when I and the Commander Mustafa Hajrulahovic, with our bodies, tried to prevent blood shed between the two sides. I tried to prevent casualties from amongst our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was that, that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date but I think it's spring 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Celo involved in it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific case that I'm talking about had Ramiz Delalic, Celo, on one side and on the other side was the commander of this brigade, Boris Krstanovic, a.k.a. Cile.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where did this confrontation occur?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the corps command. This was the Danijela Ozme No. 7. That's the street and number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were other soldiers apart from Celo and Boris Krstanovic involved in this confrontation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military police of the corps, military police battalion, and they were together with me and the corps commander, and they were there to try to prevent the conflict from breaking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what happened? What did Celo do and what did Krstanovic do and what did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command was in the middle, between these two brigades, the sabotage reconnaissance unit and the 9th Motorised Brigade, but it was closer to the command of the Sabotage Reconnaissance Brigade, and at one point, on one side of the street, Ramiz Delalic appeared and on the other side of the street Boris Krstanovic appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was wartime. Everybody was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they doing with their weapons?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Threats were made between them, that they would kill one another. Why? Well, question mark. At that point when we saw what was happening from the command, me and the corps commander ran out of the HQ and we placed ourselves in the middle between them and we said, "You can only start fighting over our dead bodies." After an hour or two of this whole mess, we managed to prevent any casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the two sides doing with their weapons when you and Talijan came down?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had taken up each window, each rooftop, every corner of the street, every place, they had their weapons pointed at each other. It was a real battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you manage to bring peace to that battle field?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply rushed out into the street. I raised my hand up and I said -- hands up, and I said, "I am not armed." Well, there were police officers with me but there was a small number in relation to the two sides. The corps commander did the same thing, and we said "We're not on anyone's side, not on the side of one person or the other. The one who begins first will be blamed, and they will have to go through us." And then by talking to the soldiers and with them, we managed to calm the situation, more or less in the same way as in the case when Caco's security deputy wanted to fire at me from a cannon. There was a different occasion. In that case and in this case we did manage to calm the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We will come to the Caco one a little later. How many -- approximately how many soldiers were there on either side, armed and pointing weapons at each other?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to give the number. In any event, more than a platoon. Perhaps less than a company. But it's hard to give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Approximately, in --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to talk about the number of pages in a document or the number of soldiers. Then you're expected to stand by that number. But as I said, more than a platoon, less than a company. A platoon numbers about 30 people and a company, depending on the kind, can range from 100 to 150 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Was Colonel Imsirevic there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure but I don't think so. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was this particular standoff between the two sides considered to be a breach of some disciplinary code of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult to describe it as anything other than that, other than some kind of disciplinary breach.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who started that particular conflict? Celo or Krstanovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic said it was Boris Krstanovic and Boris Krstanovic said it was Ramiz Delalic, and that's where things stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was any action taken as a result of this incident against either side or either man?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean, any action?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Disciplinary, criminal, investigatory? I mean, you've described a situation where you've got two groups of soldiers within your corps threatening to kill each other outside your corps headquarters, which you described as a disciplinary breach. Was any action ever taken?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I remember well the corps commander called Boris Krstanovic, Cile, to the office. I was present. The conversation lasted a couple of hours and he criticised him so much. And finally the conversation with Boris Krstanovic ended so that he said that he would not do anything in relation to Celo unless he was attacked, and that he would calm down and would not do anything outside of the permission of the corps commander, unless he was suddenly attacked. I think that the commander had a similar conversation with Ramiz Delalic. However, I don't remember attending that conversation. I think that Sulejman Imsirevic was there, the brigade commander, too, and that confirmation of this -- actually, that there was an affirmation made by the other side, in terms of this, and I don't remember whether there were any disciplinary measures imposed or whether things just ended with the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there other instances involving Ramiz Delalic and his unit on the streets of Sarajevo in breach of normal disciplinary requirements? I mean similar incidents but not involving the first brigade.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other instances like that. I can't give you the exact dates but this also took place in the course of the summer of 1993, when soldiers of the 9th Motorised Brigade and I think Ramiz Delalic was also present there when a civilian police station was surrounded, there was some kind of settling of accounts with the civilian police, or certain officers within the civilian police. Then during July, when under the orders of General Delic, Sefer Halilovic, and Mustafa Hajrulahovic, I had left Sarajevo and went to Igman. As far as I can remember, the command of the Main Staff of the B and H army was surrounded, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm interested in the "so on and so forth." You mentioned the settling of scores with civilian police. What scores did Celo have to settle with civilian police? What was the root of his animosity towards civilian police?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to say because I didn't deal with this. I didn't have time to deal with it. I couldn't deal with the relationships of one man to other people. When I had my hands full with a corps numbering 75.000 men. I can conclude, perhaps, that if it was one officer from a police station, why would I bother to surround the whole police station unless I was being irritated by something from the civilian police? There must have been some reason for it, but I don't want to speculate, because then I could just give an unobjective opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your information that he had surrounded a police station, that is, his men had surrounded a police station?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have it somewhere in my mind, but it's quite remote, and I think I read something about it in the papers those days. When you're talking about an event such as the surrounding of a police station, it's quite a minor event. It's not really very important. At that time, in Sarajevo, there were much more important things. There was a different Celo, also on the other side, who was maybe making even bigger problems. Then we had a person the likes of Topalovic, the commander of the Military Police Battalion of the General Staff. There were many others, in Stup, for example, in Sarajevo, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Describe the surrounding of a police station by soldiers as a minor incident in Sarajevo. You also described the surrounding of the Main Staff. What other things, what other incidents, similar incidents, did you know that Celo was involved in, in that period, of that nature?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't tell you more without documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there more?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless you remind me of something, then I could perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that there were more but you just can't remember them at the moment?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Celo about these breaches of discipline, that is surrounding police stations, blockading the Main Staff, threatening to killing the commander of a reconnaissance brigade outside your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did about this event in front of the corps command. These other two events, with the police and the surrounding of the Main Staff, no, I did not, because I really didn't have the opportunity later, in view of the accelerating events in the course of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you say to Celo about the incident in front of the 1st Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main thing I said at the time, and the corps commander used to send me frequently to all sorts of negotiations on all kinds of questions relating to the corps units, because the corps commander was a naval man from the JNA, from the Yugoslav People's Army. He was a diver. So he really wasn't that well-versed in the structure of the land forces. So he would always send me for all talks and to deal with problems. I mean, he knew the reasons why he was sending me out. During my conversation with Celo, the only thing I demanded was that you could not -- and it was out of the question to use one unit against another unit within the 1st Corps, no matter who it was, even if it was Ramiz Delalic, Celo, you had no right to do that and next time you will be punished in one of the prescribed ways. The conversation was also nice, in the sense of he was asked politely not to do it, but it also had its stricter side where threats were made and that kind of thing. Most often, at that time, Ramiz Delalic did listen and he made promises that he would not do things like that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, did he do things like that again?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that event in front of the corps command, there were these other two events which I recalled, the one involving the police and the other involving the Main Staff. What his participation in that, it's hard to say. I mean I have information indicating that he was present and that he did have a role in those incidents, but I didn't have the opportunity to speak with him about that later, or at least I don't remember speaking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that you told him that if he did it again he would be punished in one of the prescribed ways. Why wasn't he -- sorry, was he punished in one of the prescribed ways when he repeated that kind of behaviour, at least twice, as you've described?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was punished in October 1993. This was two or three months later, in the Trebevic operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why the delay? Why did you wait two or three months before action was taken?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to President Izetbegovic earlier and asked him to do that. Why this particular date was set, well, only the Supreme Command can tell. President Izetbegovic, and the Main Staff of the BH army, specifically Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's move to the 10th Brigade and its commander, Musan Topalovic, Caco. Yesterday you told us about Caco's area of responsibility, and at various times today you've referred to Caco being the number one smuggler and being worse than Celo in his activities. What was the relationship like between Caco and the corps command in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies but when I'm being told that I said he was the number one smuggler, a thief, a robber, I can't confirm this in relation to Caco or in relation to anyone else for that matter. I am basing all of my allegations on certain reports, certain information. What exactly was said at trial, at the district court in Sarajevo following the Trebevic operation, well, maybe this Court should request a final report concerning the final sentences that were pronounced against Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and a great deal of other people. And to request a copy of the sentence in the case against Musan Topalovic, Caco, concerning actions that he committed in Kazani and in his own brigade's area of responsibility. There is plenty more information there, I suppose. So that's why I'm telling you. There is the impression that I'm actually saying that these people are thieves and criminals but this is not something that I can assert.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber what you know, saw, observed, or heard yourself. I'll approach it in a slightly different way. What was your knowledge about Caco's background before he became a brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I never looked into that. I never tried to learn more about his life and his career. I think before the war, he was into music and he was a member of a band. So that's one thing that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he have --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what his educational background is. He may have completed secondary school or he may not have completed secondary school. But he became brigade commander, not because he would have been expected to become brigade commander in terms of the mobilisation plan but rather because he was among the first who managed to set up a brigade on his own, in April, May, and June, 1992, when the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina first started. The defence system was paralysed at the time. And that's how he became brigade commander. And no one's permission or approval was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he have a military education?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards former JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was ugly and negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did he show that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made public announcements to the effect that he was proud of the fact that his brigade did not comprise a single former JNA officer. He said he didn't trust those people, that sort of thing. And he didn't need them, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did he describe them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a wide variety of ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I should say first. I know he said things like, if he could get to the commander of the 1st Corps Mustafa Hajrulahovic at the time and then it was me afterwards, if he could get his hands on me he said he would grill me on a spit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was a former JNA officer. What was Caco's attitude towards Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said the same sort of thing about all former JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say whether his attitude to Sefer Halilovic was any different or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that he said if he could get his hands on you, he would, and Mustafa Hajrulahovic, he would grill you on a spit. Did you and the 1st Corps commander have any fears from this particular character?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very good question. In part, yes, in part no. That is the truth. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he respect the chain of command within the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a certain point in time, yes. After that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's that certain point in time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
