utterances.text: There is a document that I read here, which appears to indicate that, as early as May and June, for a rather long period of time all communication between that brigade and the corps command ceased. However, generally speaking, I can say that when I became the commander of the 1st Corps, I demanded certain radical steps to be taken by my superiors, in terms of establishing a functional chain of command within the corps itself, an operational one. Serious problems arose in relation to Caco, needless to say. The more radical I was on the one hand, the more radical he became in terms of putting up resistance on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What things was he doing which showed you he was not respecting the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say not respecting the chain of command, that seems to imply all the answers that I can think of, doesn't it? There is one thing I must admit, though. When talking about the fundamental mission of the 10th Mountain Brigade or the 9th Mountain Brigade or any other brigade within the corps, and when I say the fundamental mission, I mean being successful in defending the area of responsibility assigned or the line of defence around Sarajevo in their own respective areas of responsibility. There were never any problems whatsoever about that. Not with the 10th Brigade, not with Caco, not with the 9th Brigade, not with its commander, not with the deputy commander, with Celo or with any other units, for that matter. Brigades in their entirety and all the soldiers did their best to put up a fight and to defend Sarajevo. And in that sense, they never failed in completing a single task. Such problems as there were, were entirely outside that, were a different matter, and took on all sorts of shape and form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's what I'm specifically interested in at the moment, those problems that were outside of that. You referred to serious problems arising earlier. What were those serious problems? What sort of things was Caco doing not involved strictly in the defence of Sarajevo which were causing problems?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the actions, for example, whenever an officer from the corps command was sent to the 10th Mountain Brigade, officers or people from the 10th Mountain Brigade, based on the commander's order, on Caco's order, would be returned, in the majority of cases they would be returned because they were not allowed inside the brigade command or even inside the brigade's area of responsibility. They weren't allowed access. No matter what their original remit was or the reason why they were sent out to begin with, by the corps command. Secondly, he failed to submit reports, the reports that he was duty-bound to submit as brigade commander, and forward them through his own brigade bodies on to the corps command. Or, if the reports were sent, they were far too general, vague, and tawdry, containing no elements of facts that would be desirable in a regular military report, such as a report being sent from a brigade to a superior command. More often than not, based on all the information that was available, he randomly mobilised people, civilians, around town, within his area of responsibility. He would mobilise persons and then take them away to perform some physical labour, for the purposes of his own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about that. You've already described the official means of involving civilians in work units, requests through the corps to the Ministry of Defence, requisition and so on. Did Caco employ those official means when he needed assistance with trench digging?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were plenty of requests made by the brigade, especially in 1992, and the beginning of 1993, when these procedures were in fact used, and when he went about these tasks in a legal manner. However, there is a lot of information that appears to indicate that he did things randomly, in ways that were illegal and unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were those? What was he doing? How was he getting those civilians to the trenches?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an assumption on my part. I assume he would send his soldiers, and military police officers or some other officers, to find people, civilians, in his brigade's area of responsibility, or further afield, in town, he would bring them to the command to talk to them, and then he would send them to perform labour. How else could he have done that? They probably didn't go there of their own accord, would they?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have had some evidence even from someone who got there in that manner. But were people, to your knowledge, taken to the first line of trenches or one of the second or third line of trenches by Caco's men?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is information to suggest all of these, but anything would be very difficult for me to confirm. It's quite possible that all of it is actually true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Rasim Delic's son? Was there an incident involving Rasim Delic, Supreme Commander of the ABiH's son and Caco and his men?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I remember that incident. Among other things, as Caco was going about his business, as we just described, his son, who was a soldier, was also one of the people who were picked up, and he was taken away to dig trenches, or at least that's what people said. It took us a long time, I'm not sure how long exactly, I think several days. Several days, trying to talk, to discuss things, and we pulled many strings to get him released, which eventually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The transcript says among other things, as Caco was going about his business. Did you say Caco or Rasim Delic's son?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caco, Caco. As he was going about the business that he was going about, I mean in terms of taking people away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He picked up Rasim Delic's son?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said many strings were pulled to get him released. What was the process? Was there negotiations with him? How did he come to be released?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to think back and remember all the tiny details. I can say that I -- I had several officers in the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade. One of them -- I'm not sure if it's okay for me to say this publicly, to state the person's name, but he reported to the corps command regularly, and for the most part the information he provided was truthful. He informed on what was going on in the brigade, especially on the eve of the attack against the 10th Mountain Brigade and the 9th Motorised Brigade. He was one of the contacts used to try and get Caco to release some people. President Izetbegovic, his own contacts, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Caco aware who he had taken to the trenches? Who this person was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me this question, and this brings to mind another incident. I can't remember the exact date. I think it was in August, or September possibly. At one point in time I received a call from President Izetbegovic. He was asking me, "Who is firing at the Presidency building?" Shortly afterwards, having talked to my operations centre, I found out we had no indication that the enemy from outside the city was shooting, and our information appeared to confirm that it was Caco targeting the BH Presidency building and then President Izetbegovic said, "Is that possible?" And my answer was, "Mr. President, just about anything is possible round here, if you take into account the general military and political situation in Sarajevo." That's some sort of an answer for you. You're asking me if he was aware that he had taken Rasim Delic's son to the trenches. It would have meant nothing to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Caco in fact firing upon the Presidency building at that time? Did your inquiries reveal that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I say yes, then I appear to be committing myself. That was the information that I had at the time. It's quite probable, though, but I can't be 100 per cent certain and positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said earlier that Caco wasn't letting people into your -- sorry, people into his area of responsibility. Specifically what area was he preventing people from coming into?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area between Bistrik and the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's the name of that area?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of neighbourhoods in that area. For the most part the slopes of Mount Trebevic, the northern sector of Sarajevo. More specifically, the greatest part of Centar municipality and Stari Grad, the old town. The Jewish cemetery, Skenderija, and the entire area. I don't know all the names myself. Including Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Kazani?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kazani is a small neighbourhood near the first line of defence, or straddling the first line, even. It's a group of rocks. Kazani. I'm not sure if you could find this on a map or whether it's just a name used colloquially. It was, however, inside his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why was he preventing access to his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This requires speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What information, if any, did you receive at the time, as to why he wouldn't let anyone in, including people from the 1st Corps command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people thought the reason was he needed no one to help him defend the city. He had everything he wanted, and he could manage on his own. That was one line of reasoning. And there was another theory. The theory was the corps command was entirely superfluous to him because whatever he received from the corps command was not only insufficient, it was next to nothing, I'm saying, in terms of what he got from the corps command, in terms of equipment, ammunition, that sort of thing. Very often he used this as an excuse to explain why he had to go out and get things himself, for the purposes of his own brigade, from, as he used to say, alternative sources. Then if I go on speculating, another reason for him doing what he did, was also to keep it concealed, for as long as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Keep what concealed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of his actions, the actions that I've been speaking about, requisitioning weapons, ammunition, food, taking people away, civilians, to dig trenches, unlawful actions, and so on and so forth. When taking people -- as far as the taking away of people was concerned, the cantonal court in Sarajevo dealt with the case after the war. How many people were killed by his men at Kazani, which people, and so on and so forth. I would be hard put to specify any of that here. I've never had an opportunity to read through the sentences passed by the cantonal court in Sarajevo in these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just mentioned his requisitioning weapons, ammunition. You've already described the official means of supplying ammunition and weapons to the brigades in relation to the 9th Motorised Brigade. How was Caco obtaining weapons and ammunition outside the regular supply chain?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how. I'll describe one of the things that happened, one of many things that happened. It's very difficult for me to be specific about the date without any documents to rely on. I think it was in the spring or summer, 1993. An officer came over to see me, an UNPROFOR officer, saying they will start firing, they will tell the UN, they will tell the headquarters in Europe about it, they will do this and they will do that. And why? Because the 10th Mountain Brigade or rather Caco had taken away several of their APCs. In actual fact, what probably happened was that Caco had sent a number of his soldiers who took these APCs from the UNPROFOR people by force. They didn't kill anyone or hurt anyone on that occasion, truth to tell, but this man Caco wanted these APCs so he could send them immediately to the first line of defence, to help defend the city. His understanding of the situation was as follows. Why should those APCs be rotting away downtown in Skenderija being no use, like that? It would be much better to put them to some good use, take them to the first line, and target the enemy. The UNPROFOR commander came to Sarajevo, President Izetbegovic got involved, and I can't remember the exact date but there had to be involvement on his part. Sefer Halilovic was still at the head of the army, as far as I can remember. Rasim Delic and Sefer Halilovic had to be involved. It took several days for us to bring those APCs back to take them away from the soldiers without the use of force, and we handed the APCs and the ammunition back to UNPROFOR. That was one thing. There was another incident. He sent some soldiers over. He claimed he didn't have enough food. It was over night. And salt was carried out. He went to Skenderija where he went to people's cellars taking away considerable amount of potatoes, sacks of potatoes and commodity reserves to be used by his brigade. I had to step in to do something about it. And so on and so forth. Whether it was really his intention to use this to defend Sarajevo, to get supplies for his men, or whether perhaps this was his way of bribing soldiers to follow him in a blind and unquestioning manner, that's a very tough call for me to make. I think the best answer would be there was a bit of both in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from stealing APCs from UNPROFOR, what other means was he using to obtain weapons and ammunition outside the regular supply chain?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. Perhaps if you remind me I will tell you. I think the question is a little bit broad and unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you about what he did to obtain weapons outside of the official supply chain. You've described his raid on UNPROFOR and hijacking some APCs and taking them to the front. What other information were you given about similar activities by Caco, how he was obtaining weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was information which I couldn't confirm that there were people outside Sarajevo, somewhere in Herzegovina, that this was being purchased in -- I don't know what ways, that it was reaching Sarajevo. Then also purchases from the aggressor and so on and so forth. I mean, you could go into endless speculations and possibilities. It's possible that there is some truth in that, but at the same time, that doesn't have to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where would he have been obtaining the finances from to purchase weapons from the aggressor? I assume you mean the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to that question. I think the question itself carries the reason why. The question is where would he have been obtaining the finances from. Now, if the witness -- the witness can be asked where was he obtaining them from, and if he knows the answer he can give that answer, I've got no objection to that. But it looks as if the question accepts that he doesn't really know, but we are after an opinion. So I don't object to it being asked where the finances were coming from as a direct question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, where were the finances -- where was Caco getting his finances to obtain weapons from the Serb aggressor from?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the most difficult question so far perhaps. I don't know if there is a person in Bosnia and Herzegovina who could provide an adequate answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about the source of his financing to obtain weapons and ammunition in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know one thing: The financing from the corps command was quite modest, too modest, in fact. At the corps, in the course of 1993, I never had more than 100.000 German marks to cover the entire corps numbering 75.000 people. This is very symbolic, so symbolic that it would practically mean nothing. If I give 5.000 marks to the brigade, this is a lot of money for me, for the corps command, but essentially it's nothing. How did they get those funds? How did money enter Bosnia and Herzegovina? Who distributed it? Which channels existed? For me, this is too broad. It's too big a question for me. And I would not go into making any -- any comments on that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've described one encounter with UNPROFOR in which they stole some APCs. Were there any other encounters between Caco's -- Caco and the 10th Brigade and UNPROFOR in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such encounters, not only with the 10th Brigade but other units, to stop an UNPROFOR soldier, for example, and confiscate his bullet-proof vest, or to take communication devices which were of good quality for the use of the unit, from UNPROFOR soldiers or antennas were taken and then information would go out about that. It had to be returned. A lot of it was returned. Some things that UNPROFOR could do without were probably not returned. This was the reality in Sarajevo in 1993. Because in 1993, in Sarajevo, every person, including myself as a Corps commander, from one day to another, thought if the defence lines were broken through and the aggressor entered Sarajevo, I would never be without a bullet or a bomb or something so that I could end my own life. This was the way of thinking, as far as the majority of citizens and soldiers in Sarajevo were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they ever take food from UNPROFOR? That's the 10th I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you about a case, a little bit earlier when they broke into a warehouse and took sacks of potatoes and other staples.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about goods from private citizens in Sarajevo? Were you given any reports or did you receive any information about the 10th taking things from private civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that on a number of grounds now. Firstly, my friend has now drifted into leading and putting propositions. Secondly the witness has made it very clear as to what his sources of information are. And in my respectful submission it's getting to a point now where he's being asked to speculate, and in a leading way on matters concerning the 10th Brigade. I really do need to raise as an issue, Your Honour has now given the evidence that's already arisen, why we are going into this massive detail about the 10th brigade because you'll recall now what the evidence is and as I understand it it's effectively now finished, the crime screen evidence. That there is not one squeak of evidence that the 10th Brigade had anything to do with the killings at Grabovica, none. And although my friend -- I haven't objected up until now, but frankly I now do object to 10th brigade questions generally, and this one in particular because it's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe it is too early for us to say that there is absolutely no involvement in the killings in Grabovica, because we have to read all the documents at a later stage. So we would not jump into any conclusions on this aspect, and the Prosecution's case is not finished yet. Anyway, generally speaking, we'll allow any questions concerning with the 10th Brigade in this aspect. However, concerning with those specific questions, I believe that the Prosecution should ask about the warehouse and the actions of taking sacks of potatoes and other staples, whether those things belong to military or civilian. Depends on the question; the Prosecution could elaborate on that point, rather than directly coming to civilian properties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think the evidence was from the witness, I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, but that was UNPROFOR. I think he said that in the last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those were UNPROFOR potatoes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were those UNPROFOR potatoes?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The potatoes and many other articles that he took on that occasion, it was a few tonnes, it was quite a lot of stuff that he took. This was the Skenderija sports complex in the centre of town from where he took articles belonging to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to move on to away from UNPROFOR to private civilians. Did you receive reports that he had taken or his men had taken things from private civilians? And if so, what were those reports?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little information, and I cannot confirm that there was such cases directed at individual civilians, civilians as individual citizens, incidents in which their property was taken. The second thing is the people who were taken away, well, I don't know if they were forced to give some kind of monetary amount, but out of the numerous units from the corps, there was kind of arbitrary behaviour, in terms of taking property from companies, from firms, from certain state institutions, and so on, but this most often came down to taking motor vehicles, petrol, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say arbitrary, do you mean within the law or outside of the law?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. If we had a case, for example, of somebody from the brigade command, let's take the 10th Brigade as an example, would go to a company, having found out that they had, for example, 5 tonnes of petrol. In Sarajevo at the time, a drop of petrol was worth gold. And they got this petrol. After that, when you sent the security service to these people, and when you asked them, was this taken by force? They would say, "No, no, no, we gave that voluntarily." And then it's up to you to conclude whether this was legal or illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was Caco's relationship with -- sorry, relationship like with the 1st Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point in time, it was quite ugly and hostile. At one point, there was a clash between the 10th mountain and the 1st Mountain Brigade where the brigade commands were close by. They were about 150 to 200 metres apart. And on that occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll Just stop you. When was that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was before I was appointed corps commander. I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we go into details, could we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will take a 30 minutes' break and we'll resume at quarter to 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, before the break, we were -- you were telling us about an incident or a clash involving 10th Mountain and 1st Mountain Brigades in 1993, you think possibly before you became the commander. I want to take you through it and I want to ask you some questions about it. Were there -- where were their headquarters locations -- located in relation to each other?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of the commands were at Bistrik. I already said that they were about 150 to 200 metres apart. The command of the 1st Mountain Brigade was located in a former command building of the 2nd Military District of General Kukanjac and the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade was in a building right next to a building of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What happened in this particular clash?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that incident. It was reported at the corps command that an armed conflict was practically breaking out between the 10th and the 1st Mountain Brigades. So it was an attack by the 10th Mountain Brigade on the command building of the 1st Brigade. I ran from the command post close to that location, and when I -- on my way there, near hotel Evropa on the right bank of the Miljacka River, I was wait -- I was greeted by Mujo Zulic, the commander of the 1st Mountain Brigade, and in my conversation with the officers there, I had to take the street going along the Miljacka River next to the Ministry of Defence building, and the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade. I had to cover about 200 metres or so. Actually, very close to the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade, there was a B-1 cannon that was set up. Soldiers had taken up positions. There were the soldiers there, people were milling around. The deputy security officer of the 10th Mountain Brigade Command was there. His name was Hasic, Senad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just ask you to pause there for a moment. You mentioned a B-1 cannon. What are the dimensions of a B-1 cannon? Can you describe it to us, please?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a 76 millimetre, smaller artillery weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of damage can it do?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can cause considerable damage. It's used for large surface targets, dotted targets, and when a projectile strikes that target, as -- it can cause major damage, as any cannon can. It can also cause human casualties, as well as considerable material damage in the sense of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that soldiers had taken up positions. Describe how they had done that.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cannon crew had taken up combat positions. The crew numbers four or five soldiers, and there were other soldiers nearby. Combat position, the very term tells it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they aiming this cannon at?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cannon was aimed at the command of the 1st Mountain Brigade, but it's necessary to change the angle only slightly to turn it to the direction from which I was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that soldiers were milling around and the deputy security officer of the 10th was there, his name was Hasic, Senad. Go on, what happened.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to stop the conflict, just like in the earlier occasion, when I spoke in front of the corps command. However, when I came out into the clearing, in that street, which leads directly to the cannon, once I got to the bridge across the Miljacka I was loudly told to stop, otherwise I would be fired at. I stopped for a minute. Again, started to talk with the soldiers, with Hasic, in order to persuade them not to shoot, that they would not achieve anything by killing me, and in particular, they would not achieve anything if they start firing at their neighbouring brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And step by step, with a large number of breaks, I did manage to reach the cannon without them firing at me. That's when I stroked the soldiers on their heads, on their shoulders, I tapped them on their shoulders, because they had listened and didn't fire, and I requested or I ordered Hasic, Senad, to return the soldiers to their regular duties, and this is both in the 1st and the 10th Mountain Brigades. And this is how I managed to prevent the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the cannon aimed at you, when they yelled at you and told you to stop?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get to the cannon and placate the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed like an eternity to me, but I can't really be sure how long it took. Perhaps 10 or 15 minutes it took me to cover those 150 metres, even longer. Perhaps 20 minutes. It's very difficult for me to make an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many soldiers from the 10th were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. The streets are narrow, buildings are close together. I don't know how many of them were around the other buildings. I didn't go later to check. But the cannon crew and the soldiers around the cannon numbered about 20 to 30 altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Caco there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caco was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know what the cause of the conflict was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cause of the conflict was possibly that the 1st Corps, in the area of the Centar and Stari Grad municipalities had four or five brigades, and all the brigade commanders were people with no military experience, non-professional officers, and out of all of those brigades, only Suljo Imsirevic became the commander of the 9th Brigade later when the 3rd and 7th brigades were fused into the 9th. As opposed -- this is the western part of Sarajevo. As opposed to the eastern part of Sarajevo where there were also five or six brigades, but all the brigade commanders were professional officers, except one brigade commander in Dobrinja, Ismet Hadzic, who was not a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is the cause of that particular conflict on that particular day. Do you know what caused them to train a cannon on the headquarters of the 1st Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about that. I mean, I can give you a very brief answer to that but you won't understand it. Because of disagreement between the 1st and the 10th Brigade but what does that mean to you? Absolutely nothing. Because the answer is too short. This is why I tried to provide a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you alone when you went down to attempt to resolve the situation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the Evropa hotel there was a large group of officers. I don't want to say they didn't want to come with me but when push came to shove, I had to go on my own, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were those training the cannon on you aware of who you were, when they told you to stop?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I turned the corner, I didn't know myself, but they could see me all the time. The visibility was ideal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they aware that you were from the corps command, either the commander or the deputy commander of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasic Senad knew very well. He was aware. As for soldiers, some of them may have known and some may not have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was Caco's relationship like with Hasic Senad?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Caco had already changed his position. He didn't hang about in one place for too long. He was afraid that he might be attacked. He perhaps sensed that he might be attacked. Hasim Radelic [phoen] was his assistant for security. That would seem to imply, as was the case after the Trebevic operation, that Senad Hasic too was arrested. He spent a long time in prison sow the assumption is that he was the other man's right hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In military terms, how would one regard the training of a cannon by one brigade on that of another brigade's headquarters and then the training of that same cannon on the corps commander or deputy commander, with a threat?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under more ordinary, normal circumstances, when the whole defensive apparatus of the state was operational, when all the elements of the system were operational, when the state itself was operational, at all of its levels, there should have been a court martial. That very minute. Those people should have been given short shrift and punished for what they did. However, for a great many reasons, objective for the most part, perhaps even subjective in part, that was not taken for what it was. People decided that since there were no casualties, since no one was killed, it could end right there, and this incident was treated as just another ordinary breach of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: By that --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have taken any further steps, whether the previous corps commander or I, it would have led to nothing. It would just make the situation worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do I say that? I need to provide ample clarification, especially since you interrupted my answer. I started explaining something a moment ago. A certain number of brigades in the western part of town, and a certain number of brigades in the eastern part of town, with non-professional military men as brigade commanders, and on the other hand, you had professional military men as commanders. It was in those four brigades, in the western part of town, and we are talking about the 1st and 2nd Mountain Brigades, the 10th Mountain Brigade and the 9th Motorised Brigade. In the summer of 1993, and later in the course of the year, strategically speaking the idea was to prevent that all our brigades should become like that, to stop the 1st and 2nd Mountain Brigades from becoming like that. The idea was for the 1st and 2nd Mountain Brigades to be prevented from breaking away from our system of command. Had that been the case, a certain area would have been surrounded where there were indications that these brigades might try to secede from the 1st Corps. The reasons go very deep, indeed. It would be hypothetical to speak about these reasons. The focus was to keep the commanders of the 1st and 2nd Brigades under our control. They were important for territorial reasons because their area lay approximately but not fully between these two other brigades, the 9th Mountain Brigade and -- the 10th Mountain Brigade and the 9th Motorised Brigade. To a large extent we succeeded in achieving this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just taking you back to your answer to the question before, in relation to taking any action against the 1st mountain, sorry, against the 10th for training the cannon on you and on the 1st Mountain Brigade headquarters, are you saying -- you said you regarded it as a disciplinary matter. Why didn't the army take any action against the 10th Mountain Brigade for that act which you just said a moment ago should normally have resulted in instant court martial?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I believed is one thing. What should be done under the law is quite another. In addition, you have the third thing. What was I able to do under the circumstances that I faced at the time? These are very different things, and these propositions are very much at odds among themselves. Had I demanded that Caco be court-martialled and sentenced to death, how could I possibly have pulled it off? That's your answer. Why did I believe that this was in fact the case? My aim as corps commander was to keep, to preserve, the corps's unity and to prevent the rift from becoming deeper and deeper. The main thing was to keep the corps's mission in mind, to defend the city and the state. That was my principal mission. Everything else was less important. Another important objective was to prevent casualties. Well, our casualties at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "prevent casualties"? How could casualties have occurred?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To prevent casualties among our own ranks. Had I faced the soldiers of the 10th Mountain Brigade at the time and told them to shoot at the first Mountain Brigade, they would have done so, probably, but being a corps commander that would certainly not what I wanted to do. Rather, my objective was to prevent in-fighting and to bring about a greater degree of harmony so that the entire corps could operate successfully in our struggle against the aggressor, and in our struggle to defend the city of Sarajevo. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate for a corps commander to sometimes maybe turn a blind eye to a transgression, to a violation, if that can lead to a general improvement in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did your turning a blind eye to that particular incident in which a cannon was trained on you lead to a general improvement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the witness lass agreed that in this instance he himself did turn a blind eye to that incident. He's explained, in fact -- well, I won't make a speech. Your Honours have all heard what was said in the last passage. Your Honours, what he said about all this is "that sometimes it's entirely appropriate for a corps commander to sometimes maybe turn a blind eye to a transgression." But it has to be established that he agrees that he did turn a blind eye, and this is the - I'm working with the English translation now, of course - to this one, Before it's put to him in the way that it was. So I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the facts of this incident is very clear. The problem is we have to establish the linkage between this incident with your client, Mr. Halilovic. The witness already said that it's another matter of breach of discipline. So in the mind of the witness, he regarded as a matter of breach of discipline, rather than commission of a crime. So I wonder whether there is any point to go into the further details in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, well, as Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, was that particular incident reported to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who is everyone?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone in the chain of command, from top to bottom, and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Halilovic in the chain of command at that time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say right now, because it's very difficult for me to remember the exact date when the incident took place. If it took place before my appointment, I do believe this occurred during the summer of 1993. I assume that Rasim Delic had already been appointed to a leading position in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina by this time which means that at the time f we count the two commanders behind the deputy chief of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Stjepan Siber and Jovo Divjak, that would have made Sefer Halilovic the number 4 man or possibly the number 2 man but in terms of the army structure and in my reckoning the number 4 man of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you aware whether Mr. Halilovic was made aware of this particular incident? Either by virtue of his position or by some other means?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I believe it was the corps command that sent a report to the Main Staff, but this needs checking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the Presidency? Was the Presidency informed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the treatment of civilians by Caco? That is, of civilians in his area of responsibility. What was your information about his treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that in my -- one of my previous answers. Based on security service information, and based on hearsay, this sort of thing that people were talking about round town, he was taking civilians away, bringing them to the brigade, and forcing them to perform labour for the brigade. Later on, throughout the summer and until as late as the Trebevic operation, there was no information to suggest that he was having people killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you obtain that information later?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you or your predecessor as corps commander ever issue orders in relation to the treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honours. Before that's done, it ought to be clarified from this witness when it was that he found out about the -- the news about people, civilians, being killed. It's no use to ask did you obtain that information later, in the trial of Sefer Halilovic the question is when. That's the only way it can possibly be a relevant question. That must be clarified now with this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I disagree, because he said "later" meaning after Trebevic and the indictment period finishes at Trebevic. I can certainly clarify, I know what the answer is, but I just didn't consider it relevant to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's have a clear record at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you find out -- well, tell us about the killing of civilians by Caco. Let's open up that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Let's not open up that area. First of all, we just need the question resolved. After that, my friend can ask any relevant question he chooses. But that issue as now has to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's establish the time frame first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you find out that Caco had been killing civilians?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I received any information, if you can translate hearsay from Bosnian into English, meaning of-the-record information, started making the rounds of Sarajevo -- well, I can't give you the exact date. It was at some point in the summer of 1993. Whether it was June or July, I'll be hard put to say. However, no one was at any point in time able to confirm the authenticity of any such information or hear say and if anything at all was authentic, what? There were proceedings before the cantonal court in Sarajevo. There was a trial. This trial never resulted in anything that would show the extent of Caco's killing of civilians, and if indeed he killed any civilians, how. No such thing that I know of, at least. And still there is this persistent rumour saying that the Court found Caco to have killed civilians. There was an investigation afterwards, civilian police bodies were sent to Kazani. They carried out exhumations there at Kazani and so on and so forth. So you can go to Sarajevo and ask anyone, but no one will be able to provide you with accurate information. The first information arrived in 1994 and 1995, after the war, to the effect that Caco had killed 10.000 Serbs in Sarajevo. That's what the papers said. That's what the media bandied about, this figure, and then suddenly the figure won't down to 5.000 and then from there, as years went by to a mere thousand. And then suddenly this figure shrank to 1 or 2 civilians in some cases, or about 15 in some other cases. It's very difficult to discuss this here before the Trial Chamber, to say anything on the record. The fact of the matter is, even as we speak I do not know the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which sort of explains why I didn't actually go into this area. Mr. Karavelic, did you ever -- you or your predecessor ever issue orders to the -- your subordinate units in relation to the treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think among other things, the previous commander of the 1st Corps, Mustafa Hajrulahovic, issued an order like that in May or in June, and so did I later on. I think Sefer Halilovic once issued an order like that, while he was still the number one man in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you or your predecessor ever issue orders in relation to criminal activities, such as racketeering?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say yes, and I can't say no. I would need to go back to the files, to the documents, and have a look. I know I always talked to the security service about that. I did say that about one or two hours ago. If you can obtain official reports, worthwhile reports, based on which you can press charges against someone, please do so. That's what I always told my assistant for security. If you have information on me as the corps commander, press charges. Don't think twice. Even if it's my head on the block.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Caco suffer an injury in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, I don't think it was in combat. I think it was something that he was doing with some weapon that was not standard issue. It was something home-made. Some sort of a grenade launcher, something like that. He was testing this piece of equipment, and one of his fists was blown to bits. Some people said this had a devastating effect on his psyche. Most people said that after that incident, he became even more difficult to deal with and even less pliable for any sort of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly 1993, but can't be more specific. The summer of 1993, but I'd be at a loss to give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you say about his mental state in 1993, from your dealings with him and activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the evidence has been that he didn't have any dealings with him because he wasn't allowed to because he was going to be put on a spit. Your Honours, I don't mind the witness giving evidence about what he saw, if he had meetings with him, I don't mind him saying what that was, it could be relevant to something. The question as it's currently framed calls for expertise and seems to fly in the face of previous answers. But, however, if he had meetings with him of course he might be -- be able to say something about the mental state he observed on those occasions, so with a bit more precision I don't object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we have to establish the dealings of this witness and this other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How often or how many times did you personally meet Caco in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as I was deputy commander of the 1st Corps in 1992 and halfway through 1993, I met him personally a great number of times. I would go to his headquarters. I would hold meetings with him in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From those meetings, what can you say in your observations about his mental state?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm no psychologist, that much is certain. I'm a military man, a military professional. The main thing is those meetings, for most of 1992 and the first half of 1993, were simple working meetings. They were perfectly normal meetings. Maybe in 1993, there were a number of meetings after complaints had already started to come in, complaints about his lack of cooperation or his lack of respect for certain parts of the brigade's command chain. I talked to him and I said to him on various occasions, "Caco, don't do anything without consulting others because you and your brigade alone mean nothing. You only make sense as part of the 1st Corps. It is only if we are united that we can stand up to the aggressor and succeed in defending this city of ours, Sarajevo." That was the crux of most of our conversations. He would often complain about how little he was receiving from the corps, that he wanted to step up the struggle and defend the city of Sarajevo. I would often tell him, "We want the same thing, but you need to know that certain things just can't be done right now, for various reasons." That's what I would tell him. Until all contact ceased. He would complain about everything and anything. He would complain about President Izetbegovic and then all the way down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we are going to that document, I believe that previous document is still on the screen, and I have a question to ask of this witness, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the document on the screen. I believe it is still there. Somewhere in the middle it says, the source claimed that most of the people around Ramiz Delalic, Celo, are from Sandzak, they are mostly members of the Military Police Brigade and all of them were wearing Sefer Halilovic's badge. Could you tell us what is Sefer Halilovic's badge? I just need some clarifications.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to say that here in The Hague, when I was shown this document, was the first time that I saw and heard anything like this, that there is any kind of written record of that. I do have a vague impression in my mind that somebody at some point during the war said something about badges, but I myself never saw these badges, and cannot believe that the military police in the 9th Motorised Brigade wore these badges without me knowing about it. But there is nothing else I can say about that. And also, as to whether all the men were from Sandzak, I don't know. I don't believe that they were all from Sandzak. I don't think so. But I couldn't talk to you about the percentages of where people were from. I would have to go back to the archives to find lists of the men so that this could be precisely determined. The conclusion is that I cannot confirm this. I think here it is more a question of deliberate blowing up or making up of certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be to somebody else's advantage but I don't know to whose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise for this interruption. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, can -- can -- I'll move to another document. Can we please be shown D219? Do you have the document now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's a -- the document, just so the record is clear, is the 3rd of June 1993, it's signed by Sefer Halilovic, and is in relation to the forming of a committee. At that time, you were the deputy commander of the corps. Do you recall seeing that document at the time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could not affirm that. But I don't think that I did. It's possible but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is the --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke earlier, this is precisely the document that I was thinking of, because I've seen it here, from you, over the past few days, it's a document issued by Sefer Halilovic for the purpose of taking measures with regard to activities of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Underneath order, at paragraph 1, it orders a mixed committee of representatives of the Supreme Command Staff, the Ministry of the Interior and the 1st Corps Command to be formed. What do you know about the formation of that committee in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I might have some kind of vague recollection of this, but I guarantee that this was not the only such case. Such cases were more frequent. So I cannot really say anything specific about this commission, especially because another member, Mazlak, Enver [phoen] is a member of the commission. He's from the 1st Corps command. He was in charge of personnel and mobilisation at the 1st Corps command which means most probably that the commission was formed, and that they probably tried to get into the 10th Mountain Brigade, but because nothing spectacular happened in terms of the problem being resolved, it means that the commission didn't really achieve any significant results. This would be my assessment, and it couldn't have achieved much. This is not unusual, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why couldn't it have achieved much?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably simply because it wasn't given access to the brigade, and to carry out what it was supposed to do, according to orders of General Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we move now to document 65 ter number 16, which is 01858799. The document we are about to show you is a document in the name of Sefer Halilovic, and the relevant part -- it's to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the relevant part I want to take you to is the first page under the heading, "One, combat activities on mount Trebevic, A, combat activities of the 10th Mountain Brigade." Do you see that there now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Can you just read the -- the paragraphs under A to the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 378.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't mind this witness being shown any document the Prosecutor chooses but it should always be established whether or not he's seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, have you seen this document before you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just continue reading it, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to comment upon the accuracy of the information Mr. Halilovic provided to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance to what I know and the information that is available to me concerning this incident, I think that this is an objective, realistic, and truthful report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How would Mr. Halilovic have received this information, in the normal course of the military chain of communication?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most usual way would be for the command of the 1st Corps to receive this information. However, the superior has a right to acquire information in other ways also.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Information I've just asked to you comment on is, quote, "On the 28th of May, 1993, the 10th Brigade engaged in a combat mission of their own without the corps command approval." Quote stop. "Not a single report reached the corps command from this brigade area after the 25th of May 1993. On several occasions the corps command tried to influence the management and command of this brigade in writing through personal contacts and communication means, all too no avail, which the SVKOSBH and the Presidency have been informed," unquote. What was the effect, the military effect, the 10th Brigade engaging in this combat mission on their own without the corps command approval?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect was negative, precisely this report of General Sefer Halilovic states that the arbitrary behaviour of the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade, who on his own initiated combat, resulted in a situation where we had to activate the 1st Mountain Brigade in order to take the pressure off the 10th Brigade and the 1st and the 1st Mountain Brigade had to embark on more speedy preparations and go into attack earlier, and when it finally did go into attack, it achieved considerable effect. It took the Vidikovac positions, but after that, something unforeseen happened. There was a fog in the early morning. The wind destroyed this fog. The visibility became better, and the soldiers were visible on their positions, which resulted in a lot of casualties, as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this document objected to by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, there hasn't been an offer made to tender it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If an offer were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I don't really want to get into an auction about it. If my friend's offering it for tender, my friend should say -- is he's offering it for tender or not and then we'll say -- we'll what our position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do. I just ask him because of the break. If it's not objected to, I'll press for its tender now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask to ask -- I just ask we defer that argument until the end. The Prosecutor should offer it as he has for marking. I would like to take some instructions on a couple of aspects of it. I -- I -- I must say I already have instructions already about some parts. I'm guessing that I won't object, but I'd just like to leave that to the end if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course we will defer a decision on that document. It's time for the lunch break and we'll resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have that document back, please, which was MFI --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, I just want you to comment on the format of that document. Does it appear to you to be a document issued from the Supreme Command in 1993? Does it follow the normal format of such documents?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the signature at the end of the document, but the heading of the document seems to be the usual one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page and then the third page, please? Has the second and third page come up before you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only have the second page. Actually, the last page, with the signature, a total of two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. There should be one in the middle. Do you want to see the one in the middle?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it now. It has "paragraph B" on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's just go to the third page, please. There is some handwriting on the left-hand side of the page. The English translation says, "second tragic event on Dobrinja." Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't aware of this occurring but is it going to be sought to elicit evidence about -- about Mr. Halilovic's handwriting or somebody else's handwriting here? Because I don't know anything about this coming up, frankly. I'm caught by surprise. But if it's expert type of evidence that's sought we should know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't know either. We have to wait for the questions, I'm afraid. Would you please wait for a minute until the question is out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I thought the question was out but if you want to wait for the answer, I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question is, do you recognise the handwriting, not as an expert but as someone who may have come across it before or may not have?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise the handwriting. It doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Having seen now the second and third pages of that document, can you comment on whether it is -- appears to be a normal communication from the Supreme Command as of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it does. It has the usual format, and I had the opportunity to see various documents from the Supreme Command Staff headquarters, or from the General Staff to the Supreme Command, where events are described or assessments are given.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's move to another one. 65 ter 20, 01858798.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 379.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I don't seem to have it as yet. I don't know if I'm the only person who hasn't, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It appears to have arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know what the problem is. Would -- could I just ask for the indulgence of the Prosecutor for a minute, please, while we -- I know what's happened on the screen. It will just take us a second to fix it. And I apologise for that. We have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first question, Mr. Karavelic, as always, have you seen this document before? That is, before coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing it before, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just have a look at the format of it. The heading is "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces, office of the commander." The date is the 9th of July 1993, and just as I ask to you comment upon the format of the document we looked at a moment ago which was MFI 378, can you comment upon the format of that particular document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also the usual kind of document. I don't know who signed this document. It should be the commander of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who is -- who was the commander of the Supreme Command Staff, as of the 7th, sorry, the 9th of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The document says "A list of illegally detained persons, according to information available to the Supreme Command Staff, the following persons have been arrested and are still detained in the 10th Mountain Brigade." There is a list of 15 people. The first one is one Amir Delkic [phoen]. Did you know Mr. Amir Delkic as of the 9th of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure. I assume that Amir Delkic, under number 1 on this list, is my security officer from the 1 Corps command, one of my people, if I'm not mistaken. Even though the first time I saw this document was a couple of days ago, I remember that at one point, he was also forcefully taken by members of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Forcefully taken and what?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly what all the steps were that we took, but he was released after a certain period, and he returned to the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document -- I withdraw that. When you say forcefully taken, are you referring to taken to do trench-digging work by the 10th?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably it. I can't really explain exactly. I don't know all the details, but I do have a vague recollection that he did have some problems for a while and that he was detained by members of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are another 14 people listed on that list. Do you know or recognise -- do you know any of those people or recognise any of those names?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How could the information about those people have been obtained by the Supreme Command Staff in the normal course of military communication?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way the Supreme Command communicated with anyone from the 1st Corps usually was to communicate through the 1st Corps Command. However, the superior command, the Supreme Command, has a right to acquire information in different ways, through its services, or diagonally by skipping over the 1st Corps Command, that is their right. But this is something that was applied very rarely in practice. How could they have acquired this information? Well, there were numerous ways. There were several ways to do that. Specifically, perhaps from Amir Delkic if he was released quickly perhaps he provided this information, the first person on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the document, the first line says, have been arrested and are still detained.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a general statement. Many things were not known at the time. Never mind whether those people had just been detained, whether they were still being detained, or whether Amir Delkic was released five minutes after it was drafted, this is something that you could not specify or perhaps a couple of days afterwards. This is just general information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just go to the last paragraph, it refers to a few dozen other citizens, quote, "and members of the BH army and HVO units have been illegally arrested and detained in the area of responsibility of the 10th Brigade, where they are carrying out fortification work," unquote. Were you aware that members -- of whether or not members of the BH army and the HVO were being detained and forced to do fortification work in the same way that civilians were?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the 10th Mountain Brigade did not make any distinctions as to whether they were civilians or members of the army, if, in a given moment they were not doing anything in particular, and were perhaps seen in downtown sitting in a cafe and having a cup of coffee and there was fighting within -- with -- by the 10th Mountain Brigade they would just pick up these people because this was their conception of the proper way of doing things, to feed such people into battle or to engage them in various fortification works, for the needs of the 10th Mountain Brigade. Similarly, they made no distinction in terms of nationality. On this list of 15 people I think 14 are Bosniaks, Muslims, and only the one under number 13 is either a Serb or a Croat. I can't be sure. Also, they made no distinction in terms of who was whose son or family member or who was what, ethnicity wise. I also think that I remember that some ministers in fact were also taken to dig trenches. I cannot say specifically what ministers, at what particular time, et cetera. So it emanates, I mean the answer to all conceivable questions that you might ask me in this context actually emanates from what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not agreed to. Perhaps we could defer that particular document to the end as well, but this looks like just more of the operative information type of material, and there witness hasn't seen it so perhaps somewhat unlike the other one, I think I'll probably object to. I'd just like to defer these discussions to the ends if it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's defer it to the end of this proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, is there some specific area of objection which I might be able to cover with the witness if some further information from the witness is needed rather than leaving it to the end if he's not here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There is two answers. The answer is that first of all, it's up to my friend to do that, but secondly I think it's a fair request given that we will deal with it at the end. So I expect to object to it and the basis that this witness has never seen it before and it's operative information, it's, well, just the objections I've really raised I think would be the main ones, there is nothing else other than that there is no reason it should be admitted on the face of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I've already made the ruling that we will defer this matter at the end of the proceedings while the witness is still present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just finally in relation to that document, you've given me an answer about the attitude of the 10th towards civilians of any ethnicity and their activities in relation to taking people to dig trenches. Looking at the document as a whole, can you comment upon the accuracy, based upon your knowledge, of what the 10th was doing? Does it appear to be accurate or inaccurate, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That is a speculation. That's being sought. And I object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I press it. The witness has given evidence about what the 10th was doing and I'm attempting to elicit whether the information appears to be accurate based on what he knows or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this witness has already answered that question from the previous questions and answers. I think the picture is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we please move to the next document, which is -- it did have a marking of MFI 205. I think it -- I think we attempted to tender it through -- I don't know, might have been Mr. -- Sorry, excuse me. I think we attempted to tender it through Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll try with this witness. Can this witness please be shown that document? Do you need the ERN?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Mr. Re, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Can you see the document there, Mr. Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's dated the 6th of July 1993. It's a Ministry of the Interior document, Ministry of the Interior document headed "information," referring first of all to an attack on the police station on the 2nd of July 1993 by the 9th and 10th brigades. One moment. Earlier, you gave some information about the surrounding of a police station and the blockading of the Main Staff in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours before my learned friend commences to question on it, the initial question should be asked again, has he seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will, I promise I will ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But that should be the first question whenever we come across a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll train myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you -- had you seen this document before coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have a look at the information in the first and second paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Earlier you gave some information about the surrounding of a police station and the blockading of the Main Staff in July 1993. How do you assess based upon your earlier evidence and your knowledge of what happened in those two incidents, how do you assess the accuracy of the information in the first two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to that. With respect, the witness can't be asked to assess the accuracy of information like this because it's totally irrelevant to what the Tribunal has to decide. He can be asked whether he saw such things and what he's got to say about it. If he saw the document at the time or has some contemporaneous knowledge of it, or even something that arose as a relatively close time he could perhaps comment upon it in that regard. But to ask him effectively to authenticate what's here by saying, does it appear to him to be accurate, is attempting to lend legitimacy to a document which at the moment looks like it's not going to be tendered like all the others. And therefore I object to that being done. But I wouldn't object to questions of the normal sort that have already been permitted about what's to be found there. In other words, not to authenticate the document itself but to discuss the relevant things that have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe that that is just a form of the question. Let us go to the so-called normal sort of the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The very question I just asked was objected to while I was directed to ask have that he question before about the accuracy. I'm not quite sure how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite understand that. To me there is no difference. The accuracy or inaccuracy, as well as what he saw at this -- at that time, whether what he saw is corresponding to what is said in this document. I think this is the aim for that. To me there is no difference. But since there is objections from Defence, let's approach the normal sort of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does what is written there accord with your own information as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually have various kind information in relation to this particular event. Why? It is quite possible that at that time, if not before, I had already left the city of Sarajevo on the orders of my superiors and had gone to the mountain of Igman. So that I only heard about this entire incident in the -- it is hard for me to say anything specific in connection with this event apart from what I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Move to the third paragraph, and that refers to -- it says "According to the information currently at disposal the armed attack against the SJB premises and employees by the 10th Mountain Brigade is carried out among others by the following, Musan Topalovic, a.k.a. Caco, Senad Hasic," and there is a list of other names. It goes down, and the following members of the 9th Motorised Brigade, Ramiz Delalic a.k.a. Celo, Mustafa Hata a.k.a.
