Musa [phoen], some other names, including Molcer, Ravcanin [phoen], and finally a member called Atan [phoen]. What -- the question is the same as the previous question. Does that accord with the information you had as to who was involved in the attack on the police station?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm in relation to a number of these people whom I know, headed by Caco and a number of his people, and also people from the 9th - you said 10th - Motorised Brigade, which is who are Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and another, several other people from that brigade, but at that time, I did not have the names of those people, so that basically, my answer is practically identical to the previous one I gave you, in connection with this particular information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Move, please, to document P206?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can my friend indicated he was going to offer that one for tender. I'm not sure if he is or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have already decided we'll deal with it altogether with other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, pardon me, I wasn't seeking to traverse that. I just wondered if the practice is going to be for my learned friend to offer them all at the end or to mention now that he's going to offer them. Frankly, it's for my records, I'm just ticking them off as we go, Your Honour. That's the only reason, so if we are going to deal with the whole lot at the end I won't make the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To me there is no difference but the best way is to let Mr. Re to tell us which way he prefers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't actually going to persist with attempting to tender that one in the light of the answers just given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Grateful for the indication, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: P206, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have the next one, which is dated the 10th of July 1993, headed "security administration," and it's an official note. Firstly, is this a document you have seen before you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, maybe I misspoke. I -- I have not seen this document prior to my arrival at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just look at the information in it in relation to the attack, or the -- sorry, the planned attack. Were you aware of that at the time or became aware of it, the information contained there, or did you become aware of it at some later point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I object to that one? That appears to be one of the questions such as, "Have you stopped beating your wife yet?" It really implies the -- an answer there, so I object to the leading quality of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't quite understand it to be leading. I said, "Are you aware of the information there or did you become aware of it later."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the first part of the question is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And by the way, could the Court deputy inform us about the status of this document? It's admitted or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour this document was admitted on the 4th of March this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I appreciate you're aware of it now but were you aware of that information contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't. Not then, and not all this time after the war until the point when I read it in this document that was shown me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown the next document, 65 ter 155, which is ERN 02183086?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI 380.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have the document there now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 28th of August 1993. Under the hand of Sacir Arnautovic, your chief of security, to the Supreme Command Staff security administration. My first question is: Had you seen this document in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I want you to read the document, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it this a document which appears on its face to have been issued from the 1st Corps command when you were the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at its date and the structure of the document, if it is a valid document, it was issued by the security service of the 1 Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have the signature page in front of you, which is the second page?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whose signature is on the second page?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. Probably it is Sacir Arnautovic's signature but I can't be sure. If you have any doubts as to whether it is his signature, I cannot help you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you say about the accuracy of the information contained in the document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say one thing. That is, that most of the content of this report is something that I see for the first time now that I have read this document, and generally, this is the first time that I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What -- there is an information which says quote "The source said that the Sandzak lobby conducts many illegal dealings through Celo and Caco from smuggling deficient goods to the typical gang robberies and taking away of goods and foreign currency from civilians," unquote. What can you say about the accuracy of that particular passage?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sandzak lobby, first of all, this concept, when one refers to the Sandzak lobby, this is something that also had existed before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and people used it in their normal every day speech in Sarajevo. It was an argot concept before the war and after the war. And in fact also today. So that if I can say so, this is a concept that has worn out thin. It has been overexploited, as it were. Which absolutely doesn't have to mean a thing, but having said that, I cannot claim with certainty that there is not something there, but I cannot assert either that there is something there, nor can I say anything to corroborate the content of this document and the allegations in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is about the accuracy based upon the information you had at the time of the allegation that Celo and Caco were involved in smuggling deficient goods to -- deficient goods and typical gang robberies and taking away goods and foreign currency from civilians.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, is -- or hails from Sandzak. Musan Topalovic, Caco, however, does not. He's not from Sandzak extraction, as far as I know. But of course, that doesn't have to have anything to do with some sort of a Sandzak lobby. Now, as to the things you say they were doing, there are numerous sources that do say that they did do that to a lesser or greater extent. However, it is also a fact that these sources do not speak only about them or rather that there are sources that refer to other men and officers of the command in this vein as well. I cannot say before this Tribunal, yes, they did do that, because I have nothing in the way of compelling evidence to be able to say that, something with which I can confirm that and something by which I can stand. If you were to ask me when did Caco buy his rifle, a rifle, or sell a rifle or buy anything, I, as a corps commander, what could I tell you? I don't know the date or whether he did it or not, and how many times, if so, he did do it, and so on and so forth. But of course, most of the stories about the security service, the security service gathering and obtaining information from their sources. Now, what sources are these? This is something that only the security service knows, and I, as the commander, do not wish to venture into any guess work of that kind. Although, I often -- I often had things to say about that. I often objected to such practices. Let me tell you something about the security service and its functioning. A propos. In 1994, namely, President Izetbegovic received a letter which was about me. According to certain information, they said that I was the greatest criminal there, as the corps commander. So when this -- when I got hold of this document, myself, without so much as anyone's leave or permission, I went to see President Izetbegovic, and I could see that it bore President Izetbegovic's signature, and I asked the president, "Mr. President, why didn't you investigate this matter to the full? If I am the kind of person this document says that I am, this paper, why have not you replaced me? Or rather, why haven't you hanged me near the eternal fire in the city of Sarajevo for that? And I demand that of you now. Either treat me in this way, treat me in that way, or treat the person who gave you this report in that way." However, President Izetbegovic remained silent and would not say anything to me. So I'm just saying this to illustrate the kind of situation that obtained in Sarajevo at the time, if you capture my meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You've talked about Celo coming from Sandzak but Caco not. Where was Sefer Halilovic from?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me when I tell you that I don't know where he was born. He lived in Sarajevo. I assume that Sefer Halilovic hailed from Sandzak, just like Ramiz Delalic, Celo, did. I don't know where Musan Topalovic is from. I assume he's from Sarajevo. I don't think he comes from Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, could we move to the next paragraph or the paragraph, the second paragraph under that, which says, "According to the source's information a number of wealthy citizens are being blackmailed, they have to pay significant amounts in foreign currency in order to," quote 'have the benefits,' unquote "of Caco's and Celo's protection and do their job without disturbance." Unquote. Now, I just want you to confine yourself to what's written there and tell the Trial Chamber whether that accords with the information you had at the time about their -- about their activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I object to this. He's already been asked and given complete evidence about what he knew about racketeering and so on. He was asked those specific questions perfectly properly and he answered them. Now, asking him to comment on a document that he's never seen and made quite a point of saying he wasn't vouching for its validity is not the proper way to proceed and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And what's more, here, in this document, it says "the source claims," which means that it's not the firsthand information. It's just hearsay evidence. So this witness also testified that he's never seen this document before. That will be the hearsay of hearsay. So I wonder whether we could get somewhere through this document here concerning of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I take your point and I've moved on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 22, which is 01805241?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 381.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's an order under the hand of Sefer Halilovic addressed to the 1st Corps command of the 30th of July 1993 in relation to the dispatching of units from the 101st and the 9th -- sorry the 5th and 9th Motorised Brigades, in part, and the detachment of part of the 9th Motorised Brigade to part of the special purposes unit, the Zuka Brigade. Do you remember receiving that document in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving it because I was at Igman at the time, and a few days before this date, and a few days after, I was with General Delic and Sefer Halilovic. I was in communication with them only via radio through Motorolas and I think this is a document which they drafted at my request when, during those few days, a couple of days before or after, requested from them as my superiors to send urgent assistance to me at Igman because I didn't have enough soldiers, the aggressor would make a second ring around Sarajevo, and the aggressor advancing from the direction of Trnovo will link up with the aggressor advancing from the direction of Hadzici. I also did not see this document before, until it was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first part refers to dispatching, or paragraph 1 says, "During the night dispatch one unit from H 101st Motorised Brigade, 5th Motorised Brigade and 9th Motorised Brigade in order to stop the aggressor incursion." The second one says, "Units from the 101st and 5th shall report to the 1st Corps commander," that's you, your name is there, "and the units from the 9th Brigade shall become part of the special purposes unit, Zuka." Why was one unit from the 9th being detached to become part of Zuka's unit?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that either. The simple answer is, I don't know. It's a little bit illogical that it's written like this but the superior is always right. That's one thing. This company never became a part of the Zulfikar detachment and if I'm not mistaken the order was written on the 30th of July. The units were not able to leave Sarajevo via the airport because the tunnel was dug through only in the morning of August 1st, and on August 1st, in the morning, the Zulfikar detachment, of their own will, left Igman without my permission and they never returned to Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, what military reason could you think of as an experienced commander for the Chief of the Main Staff, Mr. Halilovic, to order the detachment of a unit from the 9th to a special purposes unit of Zuka?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a question of assessment. I would rather not make such an assessment. The superior has the right to do that, and that's what he did with this order. However, I'm seeing this order for the first time, and item 2 was never actually put into practice, and at the time, when I was at Igman, I didn't know that this was something that was supposed to be implemented, neither did I hear anything about it from anyone until I saw this document. Only on the 2nd and 3rd of August, the 1st company came out from this 5th Motorised Brigade, came through the tunnel to help me out at Igman. Later, I don't know how many days later, a unit came -- a company came from the 9th Motorised and also from the 101st and they were under my command up there. They took up the lines of defence immediately. And took up combat and prevented the aggressor from linking up from two directions. And with fierce fighting and defence, they prevented the aggressor from placing a second ring of siege around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it normal military practice for someone in Mr. Halilovic's position as number 2 or number 4 in the army at that point, to order the detachment of a specific unit from a specific brigade to another one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours I'd seek that that be clarified. Does my learned friend mean was it normal military practice in the context of the Igman war or Igman battle that was going on, or was it normal military practice in the Bosnian army more generally, or military practice in a broader context? Because those things can be quite different and in this case would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a legitimate request.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness lass given evidence that the second one had nothing to do with the Igman one. The first one was to do with Igman but the second one wasn't. My question was directed towards normal military practice of detaching subordinating units in any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I just have to expand the objection. Unfortunately, the witness hasn't given evidence that the second part had nothing to do with Igman at all. The witness says that it didn't happen, and that the Zulfikar unit vanished. He hasn't said that it has nothing to do with Igman and, well, anyway, that's the refinement. The objection is the same and yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- got nothing to add to the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The units from those two mountain brigades did not actually report to the witness himself. I believe that's what the witness testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's a different -- well we think it's a different theme but that's the reason I add the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But, Mr. Re, just ask a general question based on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question is directed to whether or not the information or the direction in paragraph 2 is normal military practice. Was it normal military practice for someone in Mr. Halilovic's position, as either the number 2 or 4 in the army, to order the detachment of a unit from one brigade within one corps to another?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please give me a little more time so I can clarify? I do not wish to be wrongly interpreted if I give you a short answer because a short answer can often lead to a different direction. The situation in late July and early August was the most difficult situation. Those two months were the most difficult ones of the whole war. And this is 100 per cent correct. You don't have to check this. The situation was so grave that it was a question of to be or not to be. The whole town could fall over night and the army could disappear, the citizens of Sarajevo as well as the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, too. That's when I requested, because I was in a panic, I was without soldiers under the onslaught of the enemy, the aggressor. Give me units from Sarajevo urgently, otherwise Sarajevo will be surrounded by a second ring of siege. And this is something that I discussed with Mustafa Hajrulahovic. I had spoken with Sefer Halilovic via Motorola as well. I don't remember whether Rasim Delic was there as well but any way they told me that everybody was there gathered together when I spoke with them, and of course they were doing all they could to get units out to me. This is my assumptions. I don't know whether Zulfikar Alispago, but allow me to be clear, more clear. I don't know whether he's from Sandzak or from Kosovo, I'm not sure. I assume he's from Sandzak. He was often in the city of Sarajevo. And what if Ramiz or somebody from the 9th Motorised said that that they wanted to fight together with that unit? At that time, it was quite normal to accommodate commanders or soldiers who wanted to fight with someone in particular. It was important to have high combat morale and to use the unit in combat to stop the aggressor. But today, ten or 15 years later, is a time when you must explain why things were done that way. If I have to be really objective, I have to speak in this way. Out of concern that I would not say something wrong or provide an erroneous assessment. I wouldn't want to do that. Secondly, it could also be a condition by someone. By whom? That's something I can't talk about because I don't know who it was. Third is General Delic, Halilovic, and Hajrulahovic would be the ones who would know exactly why there was drafted in the way it was. At the time I wasn't in Sarajevo so I wouldn't know. I don't know. I can just guess if there is something else in the background of this, but I don't need to speculate and assume that automatically it was something that was bad that was in the background of this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm afraid you did not answer the question put to you by the Prosecutor. Maybe you did not quite understand the question. Mr. Re, would you please raise it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question I asked was whether it was normal military practice for someone in Mr. Halilovic's position of seniority to issue an order detaching one unit from a specific brigade in one corps to another unit outside that corps altogether. Now, I just -- I just want to confine you to normal military practice, as briefly as you can possibly answer it, because we do -- we do have some understanding of the context here. There has been a lot of evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "normal," it means whether something was done frequently and in continuity. This particular thing that you are thinking of, I cannot say that it was done frequently and in continuity. However, I cannot say either that it was not done quite frequently. It was. So the briefest answer would be, perhaps this is not the most usual way, but the superior has a right to do it. Perhaps this is more a question for a military expert and not for a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, you did give several weeks of expert evidence in the Hadzihasanovic case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've had many, many years of military expertise, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm here as an ordinary witness. In order to respond to this question, I would have to know 100 per cent the laws on defence, the rules of service in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, about the competences and the authority of superiors. I would have to study documents in order to provide an adequate answer. I apologise, but that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the orders that Mr. Halilovic could issue as the Chief of Staff on the 30th of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to interpret that, it would be the Chief of Staff who had the right to issue orders, because he was backed by the commander of the Main Staff of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Does the document appear to you to have been signed and issued by Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it should be made clear in asking that question whether the Prosecution is asking this witness to comment on the signature and the authenticity of the document or whether he's just saying, does it look as if it's come from those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, obviously the latter. I mean, the witness isn't brought here as a handwriting expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does it appear to be a document -- you've just given evidence that you spoke to Mr. Halilovic about the things in number 1. Does it appear to be a document that he issued and signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours the same objection arises. If he's not being asked to give an opinion as to the signature, then it's a completely meaningless question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe it's about the signature. But not from the expert point of view, but from his usual practice in the past. I believe there are a lot of documents going back and forth between the 1st Corps and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And there are a lot of documents bearing the signature of Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We just want to know whether this witness is familiar with the signature of Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There is no objection to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which does not require the expert opinion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If he knows it, of course it doesn't. I agree with you entirely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me try that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Mr. Halilovic's signature, Mr. Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I'm not familiar with it but I've forgotten a lot also, but it seems as if it is his signature. But I cannot state that with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the tender of this document? If I move for its admission, so I know whether I have to go any further with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I think that my friend should assume that there may be an objection to it. I can't say that, but I'm -- he better go further with it if needs be, if he needs to demonstrate ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems that we reversed our practice but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm entirely at the party's hands on that issue, whichever they believe is convenient, we will do that. I'm very flexible on that issue. And since the Prosecution tendered that document, it's your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can respond now. Your Honours, I object to the tendering of the document. The witness hasn't seen it before. He's made comments -- the Prosecution has really got what it needs from it in the sense that the witness can recall something about the incidents of that time. That evidence is admissible and relevant. I didn't object to it, but the document itself, he didn't see it, he can't authenticate it, he hasn't dealt with it. I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the witness testified that, upon his request, this document was drafted. That means that this document is to meet his request. Secondly, the witness testified that the contents of this document, especially the part 2, he testified that whatever said in part 2 is not materialised, at least at that time. We also believe that this document has some relevance to our case and it is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P381.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I quantity to take you, Mr. Karavelic, to another area, and that is Operation Neretva. When did you first hear about an operation called Operation Neretva?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be specific about the date and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting in Zenica of the corps commanders on 20th, 21st of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the date is the 21st and 22nd. I don't mind my friend leading as long as it's the right dates. It was the 21st and 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I stand direct corrected. The 21st and 22nd of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was at that meeting or consultation. I think the question was whether the Neretva operation was discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not yet. The question firstly is your attendance there. Did you attend -- how long did you attend the meeting for, one day, two days, all of it, parts of it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the consultations began in the morning, around 9 or 10 in the morning, and it lasted practically all day. I think that I left Zenica late that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just stop you there. Do you mean -- I just stop you. You mean the first day or the second day?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first day, the 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you attend on the second day?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I did. I don't know if the consultations were held for the second day. I think two days were planned, but it was actually finished in one day. But I cannot be 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember an operation called Neretva being discussed at that particular meeting when you attended?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember it [as interpreted]. I don't think that the operation Neretva was mentioned during the consultation, at least I don't recall it being mentioned when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The transcript says "I do remember it." I just want to clarify that. Did you in fact say I don't remember it? I thought I heard -- I thought I heard you say I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago that you don't remember the exact date when you first heard about it. When did you -- was it before or after the soldiers went to Herzegovina that you heard of an operation called Neretva?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I think that I had not heard about Operation Neretva until the time when I was supposed to send in my units down there to participate in the Neretva operation, according to orders by General Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Did you attend a supreme -- did you go to a Supreme Command IKM in Kakanj? I'm sorry for my pronunciation. Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you there when Operation Neretva was mentioned or discussed at any time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that during at any of my stays at the forward command post in Kakanj I attended any such discussions or conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any role in the planning of Operation Neretva?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your understanding of what Operation Neretva was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never actually tried to understand it in that way until this time when General Sefer Halilovic was indicted. I'm not quite sure in what context you mean. I can give you my own view, my own assessment, although perhaps this is a question for an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you first heard about it when you were supposed to send your units down there, according to orders by General Halilovic. Tell the Trial Chamber about your contact with Sefer Halilovic in relation to sending troops to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of August, in very early September, the very beginning of September, 1993, I remember this, I think telephone conversation or perhaps it was by Motorola, I'm not quite sure at this point. This was a talk with the Chief of Staff, General Sefer Halilovic. I was requested then to send my units for the Neretva operation. Whether it was specifically said that it was for the Neretva operation is something that I cannot say, but what was said was for the execution of combat operations in the Neretva River valley. Given the overall very difficult, and I underline exceptionally difficult situation in Sarajevo, and of course, I appreciated that to mean our very difficult situation throughout the zone of responsibility of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, responsible for which were precisely General Sefer Halilovic and Rasim Delalic [as interpreted], and I simply tried to impress it upon the general, as far as I could, that I was afraid to actually pluck out units from within the 1st Corps formation and deploy them outside the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps to carry out combat missions somewhere in the zones of responsibility of other corps, concretely speaking, in the valley of the Neretva River. Precisely because I was afraid that a new attack might be mounted on the city of Sarajevo. Because in July and August, there was an incessant, continuous minute after minute attack on the city of Sarajevo, not hour after hour or day after day, but minute after minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I gist want to correct something. The transcript says "the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina responsible for which were precisely General Sefer Halilovic and Rasim Delalic." It says Delalic. I think you said Delic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delic, Delic is what I said. Including of course, and let me not forget the two deputies, let me not be subjective in that respect. I'm talking about the top brass of the Main Staff, the generals who were responsible for the overall situation in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was of course responsible only for the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, where was Mr. Halilovic when he -- when you had this contact by -- you think by Motorola?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was not in Sarajevo. He was somewhere outside Sarajevo. I suppose he was in the Neretva River valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he say he wanted from you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the first conversation in principle was this. Request by the general for units. However, for a time I tried, if I can say so, I tried simply to -- and perhaps it is not nice to put it that way now, in the -- before the general here, perhaps subconsciously I was trying to evade having to send my units to combat in the Neretva River valley. But today, I have to admit to my own self that I did not see the entire picture, the entire playing field, in terms of the overall situation that obtained throughout the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, irrespective of the fact that Sarajevo is -- was the capital of the republic and was the most important of all our facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which units did he want?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very soon thereafter, a written document came, indicating quite clearly the units that I was supposed to send, for the execution of combat operations in the Neretva River valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown P161? While the document is coming do you remember whether Mr. Halilovic in that conversation specified the units or whether the specification came in the order itself? Did he tell you he wanted certain units and then sent you an order or wasn't that detail discussed at first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object to that question. There could be more options than the two that have been offered to the witness there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sure he can tell us if there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll just finish my objection. The objection is that the witness has been offered two cards to choose from. It might be that there are more available in reality, so the witness could say what he remembers about the designation of the troops and which troops were discussed if any. And that's an open question that he can answer in a non-leading fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, and maybe Mr. Re you could ask one question after another.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Halilovic specify, in your conversation with him, which units he wanted? And please just -- I mean, if you can say yes, say yes, if you can say no, say no, and I'll move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He can answer it. No, I object. He can answer it yes or no but I'll move on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Unintelligible]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- answer another question. That's another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as a rule of the proceedings, the witness should first answer yes or no, if he could. If he wants to explain the reasons for this answer, he may give his reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But if the Prosecution want more information, I'm sure the Prosecution will ask further questions along this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's the other way around. I think in -- in this case, it's the Defence who want further information and the Prosecutor who is attempting to keep it under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this is the Prosecution's case in chief. If you want more information, you have the full opportunity to cross-examine this witness at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. It's just that what I really object to is that the witness be told to -- effectively to be cross-examined, have his answers limited. But Your Honour's analysis of the situation is right and I won't say any more about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You understand?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. I do not remember whether in that particular conversation he specified what particular units he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we move to P161 which I think is on your screen there? You said you received an order from Mr. Halilovic. Is that the order which you received from Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is, yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In paragraph -- sorry, paragraph 2 says, quote, "if you consider that such redeployment endangers the defence of Sarajevo I'm prepared to bear full responsibility." Is it something Mr. Halilovic actually said to you in conversation or does it appear in the order for the first time, to your ...

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to confirm whether it was said explicitly like that in our telephone conversation, but I suppose that the second point in the order stemmed from our conversation and my statements given to General Halilovic when I said that it was very difficult for me to extract my units, to send them outside my own zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And order one specifically refers to Delta Brigade, parts of the 9th and 10th and Solakovic's unit, that is the 2nd Independent Battalion, involving over 300 soldiers. Now, that's -- Mr. Halilovic has asked for some fairly specific units. Why did he ask for those particular units?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Delta Brigade, and the 2nd Independent Battalion, it was quite logical that he asked for those. Militarily observed, had I been in a similar situation I would have probably acted in the same way, because the Delta Brigade and the 2nd Independent Battalion were units in reserve. In other words mobile units of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Which is to say they did not hold the defence line. They did not have a zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the other two? Parts of the 9th and parts of the 10th.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th and 10th Brigades, from the beginning to the end of the war, had their zones of responsibility and were manning, were holding, the defence line in Sarajevo. And already, as of the end of August, I'm not quite sure whether they were included in my first order of the 18th of August 1993. I think that they were. So those brigades, in addition to this zone of responsibility which they had in Sarajevo, they were also holding a part of the defence line at Mount Igman, outside the city of Sarajevo, but still in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You said that it was logical to ask for the Delta Brigade and parts of Solakovic's brigade. Was there any military logic in asking for parts of the 9th and the 10th Brigade at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said so far, this was just for -- this was purely from a military standpoint. Of course, the superior is entitled to do it this way as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there any military logic, according to your understanding of the circumstances, prevailing in Sarajevo, to ask for those, for parts of the 9th and 10th brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an explicit and clear response to that. It is hard for me. The response depends on who is the owner of this military logic. Partly so, yes, but observed from a different angle, perhaps it is not all that logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe it's time for us to have a break. We'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of April 2005 at 9.00 a.m.
